name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Immigration losses and a Medicaid cliff test senior care system
description: We all need care as we age. Adam Scott leads New England’s largest nonprofit provider of senior care and living communities. He says demand is rising as the Commonwealth’s average age continues to increase. This week on Health or Consequences, John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute talk with Scot[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Paul Hattis & John McDonough
GUESTS: Adam Scott, president and CEO of Hebrew SeniorLife






HEBREW SENIORLIFE lost 35 employees in a single day this summer. It was the largest one-day staffing hit in the history of the senior care and housing organization, which has shed about 100 employees over the past year amid shifting federal immigration policy.  
The president and CEO says the losses compound a MassHealth financing squeeze he calls unsustainable for the long-term care sector. 
Adam Scott, one year into the top job at New England’s largest nonprofit senior care and housing provider, joined hosts John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute on a Health or Consequences edition of The Codcast. 
The 35 employees, all Haitian nationals, lost their jobs after the US Supreme Court’s June ruling cleared the way for the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians. Massachusetts is home to 45,000 Haitian TPS holders, and the state estimates at least 2,000 work in nursing facilities and home care roles. 
The terminated workers had averaged 13 years at Hebrew SeniorLife, with most working there since the devastating 2010 earthquake in Haiti.  
“These are important jobs and they’re meaningful jobs,” Scott said. “And people make a difference in people’s lives. And what’s hard is replacing that loyalty.”  
The federal travails facing the sector include changes to MassHealth, the state Medicaid system, which covers 75 percent of Hebrew SeniorLife’s long-term care patients. Scott said the 2025 federal reconciliation law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, could cost Massachusetts $2 billion a year in MassHealth funding once fully phased in. Long-term care already consumes 10 percent of the state’s $22.7 billion MassHealth budget, he said. 
“We can’t raise prices,” Scott said, describing rising health benefit and labor costs colliding with flat MassHealth reimbursement rates. 
“And so that means we have to look at ways to cut our costs and cut our costs more,” he said. “And that’s in the face of affordability challenges for every resident of the Commonwealth. We can’t cut our nursing salaries. We have to increase them because our nurses are facing rising heat costs and rent costs. And so, the rubber has to meet the road somewhere.” 
Scott placed his organization’s struggles in the context of a shrinking statewide sector: Massachusetts has lost 34 skilled nursing facilities and 3,500 nursing beds since 2020, even as demand climbs among residents over 85. About 1,200 hospital patients a day are stuck waiting for discharge because of limited space at skilled nursing facilities, he said. 
On top of the looming Medicaid cuts and sudden staffing challenges brought by the stripping of TPS status for a group that makes up a vital share of the long-term care workforce, there is a growing cost crisis facing those who rely on the sector.  
Scott pointed to Washington state’s new payroll-tax-funded long-term care benefit as one model worth watching, while cautioning that its $36,000 lifetime payout covers only a couple of months of care. 
“The middle class really has no way to pay for care except by impoverishing themselves,” Scott said of the country’s long-term care financing gap. 
On the episode, Hattis, McDonough, and Scott discuss the Hebrew SeniorLife workforce losses (6:10), the MassHealth financing outlook (14:15), and the future of dementia care at the Wolk Center for Memory Health (27:00).

 Catching Our Eye


Social Security. NPR’s Ashley Lopez is reporting, “The Social Security trust fund is running out, and yet it’s not a top campaign issue.”Congress has about six years to shore up the Social Security trust fund, which is expected to run out of reserves by the end of 2032.Enacting a solution is liable to be a significant political battle, likely involving cutting benefits for some Americans or raising taxes on higher earners, or both.
And so far, congressional leaders haven’t made it a top-tier issue.
Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno proposed raising the payroll tax for some Americans. Revenues from the tax go into the trust fund. But that bipartisan effort was immediately panned by conservative groups, and little else has emerged as a serious solution.
Civil Rights. Ideastream’s Conor Morris is reporting, “Why one Ohio civil rights activist’s sacrifice still matters today.”
Fifty years ago this month, a federal judge ordered Cleveland schools to desegregate.But it took decades of activism by parents and others — and the loss of one activist’s life — to get to that point.
The Rev. Bruce Klunder, a young white Cleveland Presbyterian minister, died in 1964 when protesting schools that remained de factor segregated in Cleveland, years after the Brown v. the Board of Education U.S. Supreme Court decision deemed segregation unconstitutional.
Lake Ontario. KOSU’s Sarah Liese is reporting, “Lake Ontario name change erases Indigenous history, Wyandotte Nation leader says.”
Chief of the Wyandotte Nation, Billy Friend, took offense to Trump’s decision to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America. The tribal nation is now headquartered in northeast Oklahoma, but has history in the Great Lakes region.Trump’s executive order claims to restore names that honor American greatness, but Friend said it is another act of forced removal and erasure. He said his ancestors, who spoke Wendat, gave Ontario its name, Ontari’io, which means “the lake is big” or ‘the lake is beautiful.”
“It’s not about politics; it’s about history,” Friend said in a phone interview. “It’s about respecting a tribal name and the people whose language gave that name to the lake.”

name: Nevada Current
title: US House Dems at Las Vegas shadow hearing link Trump ‘corruption’ to affordability crisis
description: Nevada’s Democratic House members heard testimony from expert witnesses on Friday who tied President Donald Trump’s policies and “self-enrichment” to the rising costs of gas prices, groceries, housing costs, and energy bills.  Nevada Reps. Susie Lee, Dina Titus, and Steven Horsford were featured in a congressional shadow hearing in Las Vegas focused on affor[...]
text:
Democratic Reps. Susie Lee (NV), Robert Garcia (CA), and Maxwell Frost (FL). (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada’s Democratic House members heard testimony from expert witnesses on Friday who tied President Donald Trump’s policies and “self-enrichment” to the rising costs of gas prices, groceries, housing costs, and energy bills. 
Nevada Reps. Susie Lee, Dina Titus, and Steven Horsford were featured in a congressional shadow hearing in Las Vegas focused on affordability and the cost of living. 
The hearing was held byDemocratic members of the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the House Oversight Committee, including California Rep. Robert Garcia – the ranking Democrat on the committee.
Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), laid out a laundry list of actions by Trump and his administration he said demonstrated “corruption” and “self-enrichment,” adding that those actions have exacerbated the affordability and cost of living crisis hitting American households. 
Since winning the 2024 election, Trump has created 59 companies, and he reported at least $233 million in revenue from them in 2025, according to a CREW analysis. 
“While folks in Nevada and across the country struggle with the cost of basics like gas, groceries, and health care, 2025 was the most lucrative year of Trump’s life,” Sherman said. 
Those decisions have come at the cost of Nevada’s economy, said Sherman. He pointed to Trump’s decision to host the 2026 G20 Summit at the Trump National Doral Miami golf resort, which directly benefited the president’s private business.
“He’s holding the G20 summit in Miami so that his business can benefit when cities like Las Vegas could also use the economic boost,” Sherman said.
In March, Huffpost reported that Trump’s golf trips have cost taxpayers over $100 million in security and travel costs—much of which has gone to his own resorts. Propublica also reported that a company linked to Donald Trump Jr. received a $620 million loan from the Department of Defense. 
“There’s the direct profiteering by Trump, his family, and his cronies off of your hard-earned money,” Sherman said. 
During the hearing, Titus also criticized Trump for using his public office to directly profit from selling early access to his social media posts on Truth Social, which has raised concerns about insider trading. 
“Now you’ve got the president not only buying up companies, creating companies, investing in companies, getting grants for friends’ companies, but he’s going to sell his tweets or whatever they are now,” Titus said. 
“This is really direct corruption in the American presidency. You have the president’s family potentially making — could be billions, could be hundreds of millions, by some estimates — in contracts, in loans, in crypto schemes, while the American public and their cost in gas and groceries and food continues to go up,” Garcia said.
Liz Pancotti with the left-leaning policy group Groundwork Collaborative said the affordability crisis is a result of several cost of living expenses increasing simultaneously. 
Since the start of Trump’s second term, household electric bills are up 16% nationally, said Pancotti. Fuel costs are also on the rise as a direct result of Trump’s war in Iran. Nationally, gas prices reached an average peak of more than $4.50 a gallon in May, about 50% higher than they were in February, and the national price remains close to $4 a gallon.
The average price of a gallon of regular is $4.82 in Nevada, a dollar more than it was a year ago, according to the AAA fuel price tracker.
In Nevada, the number of SNAP participants has declined by more than 20% since last summer, following the implementation of new work requirements set by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Juanny Remoero, CEO of Las Vegas-based Mothership Coffee, described razor-thin margins at her business as a result of tariffs and rising fuel costs. The Supreme Court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful and must be refunded to firms that paid the taxes on imports, but was appealed by the Trump administration.
“Unfortunately, there’s only been one importer that actually provided refunds on the tariffs,” Remoero said. “I can’t control tariffs. I can’t control gas prices. I can’t control wars, and it impacts my business.”
Ted Pappageorge,secretary-treasurer of the Culinary Workers Union Local 226, cited statistics to the committee indicating how Trump administration policies have damaged Nevada’s largest industry, tourism. 
Last year, Las Vegas saw the largest ever single year non-COVID drop in visitor volume, going back to 1970. Visitation to the city dropped by over 7% in 2025, with over 3 million fewer visitors compared to 2024, according to data from the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority.
Total passenger count at Harry Reid International Airport has been declining for 18 straight months, and the year-to-year date count through July is down nearly 7% percent compared to last year.
Pappageorge added that he believes the slowdown has been aggravated by Trump’s hostility towards allies, especially Canada, long the Las Vegas tourism market’s  largest source of international visitors. 
“It’s no surprise when you make it clear that folks are not welcome in this country that they choose to go somewhere else,” Pappagageorge said. “In Las Vegas, fewer visitors to Las Vegas means fewer customers in the casinos and hotels, fewer covers, fewer tips in the restaurants, and all that means fewer hours and shifts and layoffs for our members.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Controversial Flock cameras are found across CT. What to know.
description: The cameras capture information from every passing vehicle, raising questions and concerns about privacy and surveillance in CT towns.
text:
Towns across Connecticut are facing questions and concerns from residents about their use of automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, sold by companies like Flock Safety.
The cameras are continuously monitoring, capturing images of passing vehicles that are then used by police departments to investigate crimes like stolen cars and missing people. They serve a different purpose than traffic cameras, which are used to monitor activity like speeding or red light violations.
Here’s what to know about these cameras and how they are used.
What are ALPRs used for?
These cameras capture images of passing vehicles and record information such as license plate number, vehicle make, model, color, location and the date and time the vehicle was photographed. Some systems can also identify characteristics of a vehicle even when its license plate is not visible.
Police can search ALPR systems for vehicles connected to an investigation or receive alerts when a vehicle on a law enforcement watch list passes a camera. Investigators can also search for vehicles that were in a particular area when a crime occurred.
But because the cameras, which don’t use facial recognition technology, capture information from every passing vehicle, they have raised questions about privacy and surveillance.
The companies that sell the cameras, like Flock Safety, have examples on their websites of times the cameras have proven useful to police. But there is little information available about how effective the technology is in Connecticut specifically.
Who determines where these are installed?
Individual cities and towns decide whether to install the cameras, which technology to use and how long to keep the systems.
That means the number of cameras, the vendor and the policies governing their use can vary from one community to another. A Flock Safety spokesperson recently told Connecticut Public that at least half of the state’s police departments use some of the company’s services, including the license plate readers and drones.
Some Connecticut communities have in recent months paused or reconsidered additional installations amid resident concerns about privacy and data sharing.
Gov. Ned Lamont has also asked municipalities to pause new camera installations while state officials develop additional guidance.
Are ALPRs the same as traffic cameras?
No, and automated license plate readers are not used to enforce traffic laws.
ALPRs are different than traffic cameras because they are not triggered by an action like speeding. The cameras continuously capture vehicle information.
How long is the information kept?
Privacy advocates have raised concerns about what happens when individual vehicle sightings are collected over time. A network of cameras can potentially provide a broader picture of where each vehicle has traveled.
A new law in Connecticut was signed in May and includes some provisions that go into  effect in October and beyond. It attempts to address those concerns by limiting how long ALPR information can be kept and how it can be used. Under the law, agencies generally must delete data after 21 days unless it is tied to an active criminal investigation. 
Can police share the information?
Yes, but there are restrictions.
The new Connecticut law prohibits ALPR data from being used for immigration enforcement. It also restricts its use in certain investigations involving reproductive healthcare, gender-affirming healthcare and activities protected by the First Amendment.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ House candidates increasingly skip League of Women Voters debates
description: Congressional candidates in both parties are more likely than ever to dodge debates planned by the League of Women Voters.
text:
Republican Michael McGuire, left, is seeking to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway (D) this fall in the 3rd Congressional District, and McGuire claims Conaway is ducking a planned debate. (McGuire photo courtesy of his campaign/Conaway photo by Dana DiFilippo/U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray)The League of Women Voters, a century-old nonpartisan voting-rights organization, has long hosted public debates around the country as a way for citizens to engage with the political candidates running to represent them.
But in recent years, the number of candidates on both sides of the aisle who duck their debates has climbed, with GOP officials in Cape May County urging Republicans up and down the ballot this year to avoid league events altogether.
To Jesse Burns, who heads the league in New Jersey, the trend is equal parts troubling and baffling, especially as participation in voter guides produced by the group wanes too.
“We have refusals across the state right now,” Burns said. “We’re just looking to provide information to voters so that we can increase voter turnout and have voters feel confident that they have the information they need to cast a ballot and actually understand what candidates’ policies are and not just the party that follows their name.”
Feud escalates between NJ governor, GOP over voter registration gaffe

Election observers say debate-dodging is a longtime campaign strategy that has become more common in the social-media era as candidates — especially incumbents and front-runners — try to avoid gaffes that could go viral and cost them votes.
That happened earlier this month, when Republican Sen. Darline Graham — facing a runoff election to retain her late brother Lindsey Graham’s U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina — flubbed a question about national security in Taiwan and the South China Sea.
“National security is not my thing,” she said in a moment that earned her widespread drubbing on social media. “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham prevailed despite the debate stumble.
A gotcha moment during a New Jersey gubernatorial debate last fall echoed long after Democrat Mikie Sherrill, who went on to win, and Republican Jack Ciattarelli left the stage. Sherrill accused Ciattarelli, a former medical publisher, of killing “thousands” of people by printing propaganda for the opioid industry.
“A lot of people thought that moment was over the top, and there were questions about whether it was a fair charge or whether it was a distorted charge,” said Micah Rasmussen heads the Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics at Rider University. “But it put him on the defensive for the rest of that debate, and really after the debate. He had to answer those questions at a time when he needed to be on the offense.”
Those debate moments show why some candidates prefer to play it safe, steer clear of the debate stage, and carefully control their messaging, Rasmussen said.
“Most of the time, modern campaigns are designed around that scripted moment, and debates are essentially that one time when it’s not scripted, when you could be asked a tough question,” he said. “It’s a high-risk, low-reward situation for a lot of candidates who are ahead, and they would just rather run out the clock.”
But skipping debates can backfire because it gives a candidate’s campaign rivals ammunition to attack, as Republican Michael McGuire did last week in his bid to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway, the Democrat incumbent in Burlington County’s 3rd Congressional District. McGuire blasted Conaway for skipping a League of Women Voters debate.
“For more information — or if you’re Congressman Conaway changing your mind about debating — please contact the campaign,” McGuire’s team cheekily wrote in a news release.
Conaway didn’t respond to the New Jersey Monitor’s request for comment. He told the league’s Monmouth County chapter he had a scheduling conflict, said chapter spokeswoman Mary Donnelly. McGuire also did not confirm his participation, Donnelly added. McGuire’s team told the New Jersey Monitor he sent the chapter a letter indicating he would participate if the forum is held in person before Sept. 19, when ballots begin going out.

“The most effective attack you can make against an incumbent is that they’re not doing their job, and voters broadly perceive engaging with the public as being part of doing your job,” said Dan Cassino, a political science professor and pollster at Fairleigh Dickinson University. “So if you dodge debates, this opens you up to attacks: ‘Oh, this person’s afraid of us. This person won’t speak to the public. This person won’t reveal their views.’”
In Cape May County, GOP chair Michael Donohue said his guidance to Republican candidates to avoid league events there has more to do with local leadership, which he does not regard as nonpartisan, rather than opposition to the group broadly.
“They are very vocal. And — God bless them — I’m not saying they’re doing anything wrong by being far to the left. That’s their prerogative in a free country. I’m just saying that from the standpoint of a Republican candidate, why would you go to a forum hosted by those folks?” Donohue said.
Burns denied any bias and pointed to debate format as proof why partisan fears are unfounded.
“League debates are pretty standard,” she said. “In general, it is a league moderator asking questions that we get from the audience, which is community members. And these are not gotcha questions. These are usually questions like, ‘What are your policy priorities and why?’ So it’s not like we’re setting candidates up to fail in these debates.”
Bias questions aside, Donohue said he struggles to see the point of debates at a time when journalism is shrinking and people are getting their information from a wider array of sources.
“I don’t hate debates, but there’s an analysis from a campaign political standpoint: What’s the value?” Donohue said.
Donohue has run for state Assembly twice and served as his county’s GOP chair since 2010, except during a four-year stint as a state Superior Court judge. He said candidates used to embrace debates in hopes of landing media coverage that would deliver their message far beyond the voters in the debate audience. But now, many news outlets don’t air or cover debates, and even social media can’t reach all the voters a candidate — especially at the local level — can reach by knocking on doors and other such activities, he said.
“Debates end up being just a discussion to your supporters,” he said. “There’s rarely any serious substance in these things, and even if they ask questions that should get substantive answers, typically the candidates just pivot back to some hot-button issue that they want to push to the base. We’re in this Twitter/X moment, and everybody just wants these little sound bites.”
Cassino also sees broader trends at play.
“Debates really are an invention of the TV era, and so it’s possible that they’re going away as the TV era comes to an end,” he said.
Voters increasingly rely on partisan cues as politics becomes hyper-polarized, rather than investing time in listening to debates or seeking out other unfiltered sources of information about candidates, he added.
“In some sense, voters don’t need as much information because the partisan heuristic is more powerful than it’s been in the past,” Cassino said. “So, if I’m a Democrat: ‘I don’t need to know anything about Democratic candidates. They could be the worst candidate on earth, and I’m going to vote for them anyway.’ Most voters are really just: ‘I’m a Democrat. I’m a Republican. Therefore, I know who to vote for.’”
Independent voters still have to do their homework to learn about candidates, he said.
But, he added, “I’ve been teaching college for 20 years. I can tell you nobody likes doing homework. So those voters, by and large, just don’t turn out to vote at all.”
Voters should pay attention when candidates dodge debates, though, Rasmussen said.
“They should want candidates who are accountable, and this is one more form of accountability,” he said. “It’s one more form of: ‘I’m not afraid to answer questions. I’m not afraid to have you measure me up against my opponent. Ask me anything you want.’ That kind of accountability is what we should all want from our elected officials.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Mystery price tag: Utah can’t say how much it’s losing from data center tax break
authors: Sydnee Chapman, The Utah Investigative Journalism Project
description: The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch. States are forgoing millions and, in some cases, billions of dollars in revenue by allowing data centers to skip out on paying sales tax.  But Utah has no idea how much money it’s losing to these tax exemptions […]
text:
Construction continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain on Friday, April 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch.
States are forgoing millions and, in some cases, billions of dollars in revenue by allowing data centers to skip out on paying sales tax. 
But Utah has no idea how much money it’s losing to these tax exemptions — the state simply doesn’t collect the data. That’s thanks to legislative action nearly two decades ago that repealed reporting requirements. 
That gap in transparency is sparking doubts about whether policymakers can adequately evaluate the tax exemption program at a time of heightened public interest in data centers and their impacts on the state. 
“The scale and rapid growth of data-center investment raise legitimate questions about whether our current framework, and the data available to evaluate it, remain adequate,” Rep. Jill Koford, R-Ogden, said in an email. Koford sponsored a bill passed by the Legislature earlier this year requiring transparency around data centers’ water usage. 
Utah isn’t alone in its opaque approach to sales and use tax exemptions for data centers. A report from Good Jobs First, a nonprofit which focuses on corporate and government accountability, found that 14 of the 37 states with such exemptions don’t publish their official revenue losses in a timely manner. Those that do reported losing between $830,000 and $1.9 billion in 2025, with larger losses projected for this year and beyond. 
In Utah, the higher end of that range would be nearly half of the total amount the state collected in sales and use tax last year. That amount is a drop in the bucket of the state’s $37 billion budget, but it’s still enough to pay for significant benefits. It would, for example, cover a sizable gap in the state’s Medicaid budget and quadruple the amount lawmakers allocated for a first-time home-owner program this year  — and still have over $1.6 billion left over.  
Meanwhile, the lower end of the spectrum, $830,000, would be enough to pay the governor’s annual wages and benefits for over three years. 
Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain on Friday, April 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Kristian Fors, an analyst with the Utah-based Libertarian think tank Libertas Institute, stressed the need for Utah to track these incentives. 
“You can’t manage what you can’t measure,” he said. “For any government policy, transparency and accountability is of utmost importance.”
Kasia Tarczynska, who authored the Good Jobs First report, said many states created these sales and use tax exemptions based on the smaller-scale data centers that existed 10 to 15 years ago but that those programs have skyrocketed in the past few years due to artificial intelligence deployment. 
“This program did not change at all, but the industry has changed to the point that it’s a very, very different industry,” Tarczynska said, adding that this mismatch calls for states to review these programs. “We’re seeing this explosion in subsidy costs. That’s why it’s extremely important for state governments and for state lawmakers to go back, pause these programs … and even figure out if it makes financial sense for the state to even provide these subsidies.” 
Some states are doing just that. Governors in Nebraska, Ohio, Illinois and Massachusetts announced pauses on tax incentives for data centers.
Tarczynska stressed that these kinds of tax breaks don’t play a large role in where companies decide to locate data centers. Instead, she said, the focus is on electricity prices, fiber connectivity, cheap and available land, low regulations, water access and stable climate. 
“Subsidies kind of come at the end of the site selection process, and they don’t really have a big impact on a location decision — they’re kind of like a bonus, like a cherry on top,” she said. “They’re already spending billions and billions of dollars — spending maybe 2% more on paying their fair share in taxes is not going to change their calculations.” 



Quotation







You can’t manage what you can’t measure. For any government policy, transparency and accountability is of utmost importance.


– Kristian Fors, Libertas Institute analyst


Khara Boender, a spokesperson for Data Center Coalition, the industry’s trade group, pushed back against that notion but said it’s difficult to say what the hierarchy of deciding factors is. 
She pointed to Virginia, which is home to one of the largest data center markets in the world, as a counterpoint. The state’s legislative audit and review commission found in a 2019 review that the majority of data center investments in Virginia wouldn’t have occurred without tax exemptions. 
“I think that’s one specific stat that pushes back on that notion that these are not being decisive factors in where data centers are locating,” Boender said. “One of the things to look towards is also the different economic contributions of the data center industry, especially if we’re looking at why a state might want to offer an exemption package to try to attract that type of investment.”
A decades-old decision playing into the AI boom 
The framework for the Utah program was revamped in 2009 when the state Legislature passed a law doing away with the requirement for businesses, individuals and nonprofits to report transactions that are exempt from state and local sales taxes. 
At the time, the Utah Tax Commission used those reports to compile the total amounts of those exemptions and turn them over to the Legislature to aid in policy decisions. However, reporting was hit or miss, making the data unreliable, according to Utah State Tax Commission Deputy Executive Director Jason Gardner. 
“The focus at the time was traditional manufacturing and semiconductor-related equipment exemptions; modern hyperscale AI data centers were not contemplated in that discussion,” Koford said. “That history matters because the reporting change has left us with limited visibility into the actual fiscal impact of the equipment exemption as applied to today’s large data centers.” 
The northern shores of the Great Salt Lake are visible at the back of a swath of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, that is part of the proposed Stratos Project data center, is pictured on Wednesday, May 27, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The bill also directed the commission to produce annual estimates on sales and use tax exemptions, but Gardner said it is unable to do so for categories where a small number of companies are utilizing the exemption, including data center machinery and equipment. 
Tarczynska said estimates from state agencies on how much the exemptions cost taxpayers are often far lower than the true value. She added that a handful of states that haven’t previously tracked the exemption costs conducted special studies focused on data centers and the subsidies. But those one-time reports raise their own red flags.
The lack of transparency, she said, is “a cautionary story.” 
“There are other industries that have their own sales and use tax exemption. We don’t know what the future brings, right? So therefore, every subsidy program needs to have very smart, targeted requirements and company obligations, including not only in job creation, creating good quality jobs, but also in reporting.” 
Fair treatment?
Utah’s sales and use tax exemption program covers a wide range of categories beyond just machinery, equipment or parts purchased by data centers. Other exemption categories include sales to or by churches and charities, aircraft manufactured in the state and certain construction products sold between related entities. 
“This policy acknowledges the capital-intensive nature of data center investments and aligns data center tax treatment with that of manufacturing equipment, which enjoys similar exemptions in 41 states,” said Boender with the Data Center Coalition. She declined to comment on how a reporting requirement for the exemptions would impact the industry.
Koford said the goal of these kinds of exemptions is to prevent companies from being taxed more than once as goods move through the supply chain rather than bonus incentives for businesses. 
Libertas Institute analyst Fors argued that “fair” tax policy is consistent across the board, regardless of industry. 
“We shouldn’t have favoritism in government policy,” he said, adding, “We don’t want the government choosing winners and losers.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Developmental disabilities program for WA families to be cut, but not ended
description: Washington state officials are keeping a longstanding program seen as vital to parents of children with developmental disabilities, but cutting its funding, ending weeks of unease about its future.  The state Department of Social and Health Services is trimming the Parent to Parent program by 10%, but won’t eliminate it as was feared this summer. […]
text:
The state Capitol in Olympia, Washington on Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)Washington state officials are keeping a longstanding program seen as vital to parents of children with developmental disabilities, but cutting its funding, ending weeks of unease about its future. 
The state Department of Social and Health Services is trimming the Parent to Parent program by 10%, but won’t eliminate it as was feared this summer. Its budget for the next year is around $877,000. 
“I wish we hadn’t received a cut at all, but it certainly could have been worse,” said Tracie Hoppis, the statewide Parent to Parent manager.
Department of Social and Health Services spokesperson Jessica Nelson said the agency continues “to work to protect core services and ensure that Washington has a solid financial foundation for the long-term.”
The episode provides a glimpse into the types of cuts Washington leaders will need to consider as they face ongoing budget woes. In the coming weeks, state agencies will make their requests to Gov. Bob Ferguson in the upcoming two-year spending plan he’ll put forward in December. 
Ferguson has pledged not to propose tax increases, and has instead said he’ll look to fill the state’s latest budget shortfall by cutting spending from newer programs, though Parent to Parent has been around for decades.
Parent to Parent provides support and resources for families of children with autism and other developmental disabilities. Its name comes from pairing newer parents with more experienced ones to help guide them through the complicated system of available resources, as well as provide community in what can otherwise be an isolating experience. It also features “sibshops” to support siblings of people with developmental disabilities.
The first Parent to Parent program in Washington was established in 1980 in King County. Today, it serves families of children and adults in all of Washington’s 39 counties, with tens of thousands of calls and emails for assistance every year
Program advocates were shocked to learn Parent to Parent was on the chopping block with a contract only through August, despite funding in the state budget. The Arc of Washington State oversees the statewide program under a contract with the state Department of Social and Health Services.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
If the state didn’t extend the contract, Parent to Parent would’ve ceased to exist, leaving families to traverse the complicated web of services with less support.
Supporters of the program were especially frustrated the funding could be cut outside the legislative process, without public input.
Given this, a bipartisan group of 44 state lawmakers urged Ferguson and Department of Social and Health Services Secretary Angela Ramirez to maintain the program.
Hoppis thanked these elected officials and others for helping secure the program’s future.
“I feel really overwhelmed and a bit humbled with the level of support that we received,” she said.
The 10% reduction will partly trim spending on multicultural coordinators, who help parents overcome language and other barriers, said Hoppis, who leads a Parent to Parent program in Yakima County. Many families in the program are Spanish speakers. And in Snohomish County, for example, a Parent to Parent program has a Russian coordinator. 
“When it comes to Parent to Parent and the emotional support piece, that does not happen well through an interpreter,” Hoppis said.
Broadly, reduced funding means the program potentially serves fewer families.
Advocates are asking legislators to reverse the cut and provide a modest increase in 2027. They also want Parent to Parent named specifically in next year’s budget, so the money can’t be redirected elsewhere.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Trump’s trade war with Canada is reckless, pointless and dangerous
description: President Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada isn’t about our northern neighbor not playing fair. Rather, it’s the story of a bumbling president desperate for a win. He sees Canada as a weak economic target and thinks he can crush it.  A bully’s gonna bully. But Trump’s intimidation tactics haven’t worked very well lately.   His war on Iran, which Trump p[...]
text:
Ambassador Bridge (Photo by Ken Coleman/Michigan Advance)President Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada isn’t about our northern neighbor not playing fair. Rather, it’s the story of a bumbling president desperate for a win. He sees Canada as a weak economic target and thinks he can crush it. 
A bully’s gonna bully. But Trump’s intimidation tactics haven’t worked very well lately.  
His war on Iran, which Trump predicted would be won in two or three weeks, has entered its sixth month with no resolution in sight. Russia’s war against Ukraine, which Trump said multiple times that he could end on his first day in office, has dragged on for more than four years. Greenland is still a Danish territory despite Trump’s repeated threats to use military force, if necessary, to acquire it. 
Inflation remains stubbornly high. Americans are fed up with the escalating cost of food, gasoline and housing. Trump has no answers except to continually blame his predecessor, former President Joe Biden. 
So what does he do? Engage the United States in what could become a dangerous, all-out trade war with a country that long has been one of our most-valued economic partners. 
It’s reminiscent of Michael Moore’s 1995 comedy, “Canadian Bacon.” The movie tells the story of an unpopular president who tries to boost his moribund approval rating by engaging in a cold war with Canada. “Surrender pronto, or I’ll level Toronto,” the U.S. president, played by Alan Alda, threatened. Almost as farcical, Trump has signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”  
The U.S. and Canada called off trade talks just hours before 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports to the U.S. kicked in on Aug. 22, with both sides blaming each other for the failure to reach an agreement.
President Donald Trump holds up a chart while speaking during an event announcing broad global tariffs in the Rose Garden of the White House on April 2, 2025.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
The tariffs will cost U.S. consumers more to buy hundreds of Canadian goods, including hockey sticks, dairy products and furniture. Three days later Canada retaliated with tariffs on $20 billion of U.S. goods, slated to start on Sept. 8. Tariffs will range from 15% to 50% on appliances, metals, lumber and hundreds of other products. Trump is threatening to double tariffs on all cars and auto parts imported from Canada to 50%, up from 25%, starting in January.  
The proposed tariffs likely violate the United States, Mexico, Canada free trade agreement, which Trump negotiated in 2020. But ignoring legalities is one of the president’s special talents. 
Trump claims Canada has been “ripping off” the U.S. for years. But the U.S. runs a trade surplus in nonenergy goods and services with Canada.  Michigan could pay a steep price for Trump’s reckless actions. Canada is Michigan’s largest trading partner with about $70 billion in goods flowing across their borders in 2024, the latest available data. Thousands of jobs are connected to Michigan auto parts manufacturers, farmers and others who export goods to Canada. 
Trump not only doesn’t care, he has said he would use “economic force” to cripple Canada and make it our 51st state. Vice President JD Vance reiterated that goal on August 24 when he said in a speech, “Canada is a state,” and then unconvincingly said he’d made “a Freudian slip.” 
The president has said on numerous occasions that he wants Detroit’s automakers to stop building cars and trucks in Canada and move that production to the U.S. Trump has repeatedly said the U.S. doesn’t need Canada for anything. (Funny, he has said the same thing about the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran is choking off critical oil supplies.) SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The president’s economic attacks on Canada are said to be personal. He had a contentious relationship with former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, which led to the president slapping tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. The president’s dealings with current Prime Minister Mark Carney, the cerebral former central banker, aren’t much warmer.  After trade negotiations collapsed, Carney said Canada would never accept the idea that the country is a “subsidiary of the United States.” 
And Trump may have met his match in insult trading with bombastic Ontario Premier Doug Ford. “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so (Trump) has a lot of room to kiss my ass,” Ford said after the trade talks failed. 
Ford also threatened to pull the plug on Ontario’s hydropower-generated electricity it sells to the U.S., an indication of just how serious the economic rift between Canada and the U.S. has become. Canada’s “elbow’s up” trade stance against Trump carries a great deal of risk for a country that has an economy one-twelfth the size of the U.S. economy.
Some experts say tariffs on their exports could price many Canadian companies out of the U.S. market, putting thousands of jobs at risk. But a savvy Carney is wisely cultivating new markets for Canadian goods and services around the globe. The U.S., he has said, “is no longer a reliable partner.” 
Canada and the U.S. have been friends and beneficial trading partners for centuries. It’s outrageous that a greedy, petulant U.S. president is doing his best to destroy that relationship.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Medicaid spending is accelerating, projected to reach $29B in 2029
description: Minnesota’s spending on Medicaid is projected to far outpace the state’s growth in tax revenue over the next several years, underscoring the urgent challenge posed by federal cuts to a state budget already strained by rising healthcare costs and a growing elderly population. The state’s Medicaid program, which insures many low-income, disabled, elderly and p[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)Minnesota’s spending on Medicaid is projected to far outpace the state’s growth in tax revenue over the next several years, underscoring the urgent challenge posed by federal cuts to a state budget already strained by rising healthcare costs and a growing elderly population.
The state’s Medicaid program, which insures many low-income, disabled, elderly and pregnant residents, is on track to jump 40% over the next four years to $29 billion while state revenues are expected to increase just 10% over the same period.
Medical Assistance, the name for Minnesota’s Medicaid, cost $20.3 billion in fiscal year 2025, roughly split between state and federal dollars. The cost is projected to jump to $24 billion for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in June — costing around $4,100 per every Minnesotan and $20,000 for each of Medicaid’s 1.2 million enrollees.
The next governor and state Legislature may be forced to make difficult choices: raise taxes, curb the growth of the program, which could affect patients — especially the elderly — or see Medicaid eat into other key priorities like education or infrastructure.
Even as the sprawling program is getting more expensive, provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the Trump administration’s targeting of Minnesota, ostensibly over widespread fraud, are worsening the funding picture. The result is a shift of these higher healthcare costs onto the state, healthcare providers and patients.
Spending on the program is accelerating faster than what budget officials predicted in early 2025. The total receipt for Medicaid spending this past fiscal year has yet to be released, but the most recent projection from February is $2 billion higher than what state officials predicted in 2025.


While seniors are often insured through Medicare, Medicare doesn’t generally cover long-term care in nursing homes or home care. Instead, Medicaid, which is more widely known as the health insurance program for low-income adults and children, makes up the bulk of public spending on long-term care for seniors and people with disabilities.
In Minnesota, seniors and disabled people make up around a quarter of Medicaid recipients but  over 60% of Medicaid spending, which includes long-term care as well as “basic care” like doctor’s visits and medications. This is in line with national trends.
Much of the jump in predicted Medicaid spending comes from higher spending for direct care, according to the state’s budget office.
Around three-quarters of that increase came from people using more services, and the remaining quarter came from services costing more. Budget officials pointed out that the one “notable exception” to this is that the increase in spending on drugs mostly has to do with people using more expensive medication — as opposed to people using more medication in general.
A smaller but still significant portion of the increase came from higher spending on long-term disability services outside of institutions like nursing homes. Those services include basic living assistance and help finding a job. Both the number of people signing up for those services and the costs of long-term care services grew more than expected in 2025, leading to higher future projections.
Several long-term care services for disabled and elderly Minnesotans have been identified as “high risk” for fraud, waste and abuse by the Walz administration. Spending in some of those services more than doubled in the past few years — some of that increase came from intentional effort from the state to keep people out of institutions.


Those “high-risk” services are now at the center of the ongoing funding fight between the state and the Trump administration, which threatened to cut $2 billion annually in Medicaid funding over program integrity. The Walz administration’s human services department has since scrambled to implement program integrity measures demanded by the Trump administration, at times to the detriment of broad swaths of care providers and their clients.
The Trump administration’s Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has also repeatedly  clawed back past Medicaid payments, totaling $549 million over the past three quarters. In late July, the federal agency announced its most recent effort to freeze money for services from January through March. The Trump administration has offered little indication that it intends to stop for future quarters.
The Minnesota Department of Human Services said in a statement that it hasn’t interrupted payments to providers as a result of the $549 million freeze, but that the possible total annual $2.5 billion freeze “is not an amount the state can cover indefinitely without impacting services.”
Federal officials said they would release the $2 billion after the state implements its CMS-approved “corrective action plan,” which could take until March 2027.
John Connolly, the state’s temporary commissioner of human services, said in March that the Medicaid clawbacks would cause significant cash flow issues to the state budget, which “could disrupt payments to providers, strain hospitals and long-term care facilities, jeopardize services for vulnerable populations, and destabilize care.”
Medicaid is still operating as usual, and any changes to eligibility and services would require actions from both the Legislature and the governor.


The February state budget outlook didn’t take into consideration how the recent threats to Medicaid funding will affect the state’s bottom line.
As of November 2025, the budget outlook did begin including a few small fiscal impacts from the 2025 federal budget bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. An end-of-session budget update includes more of OBBBA’s impact, after the 2026 Legislature brought state law into alignment with federal law.
The impacts of OBBBA-related state legislation don’t make much of a dent though.
New state legislation reduced the state’s share of Medicaid spending by 0.1% for the current biennium — the state’s two-year budgeting period — and by 2.4% for 2028 and 2029. In other words, not much. And the largest savings come from new billing limits that are not related to OBBBA, according to the state’s budget office.
Although Medicaid is a shared federal-state program, OBBBA’s savings to the federal budget don’t always translate to savings for the state.
Minnesota’s budget outlook improves

For example, the Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare, expanded Medicaid to cover adults who make between 100% and 138% of the federal poverty line in many states, including Minnesota. The federal government foots the bill for 90% of the care for those adults.
New work requirements in OBBBA make those Medicaid expansion recipients prove that they work or volunteer if they’re able to, starting in 2027. The work requirements are expected to lead to people losing Medicaid, which is the main way OBBBA lowers federal spending on the program.
But new work requirements will also likely cause some of the expansion recipients to switch from being eligible based on income to being eligible based on disability to avoid the administratively burdensome requirements, according to the state’s budget office. Their healthcare would then be funded roughly equally by the state and federal government, meaning the state would pay for more of their care than previously — a win for the federal budget, a loss for Minnesota.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Advocates call for further reform to Mississippi tenant laws
description: Lily Coleman said she has lived at Addison Place Apartments since 2018 and this was the first time her water had been shut off. Coleman said her family is saving money so they can move.
text:
Housing advocates are pushing for stronger protections for Mississippi renters, arguing state law leaves tenants with limited options when problems with their housing go unresolved. 
Tenants generally cannot withhold rent over needed repairs, and state law limits when they can make repairs themselves and recover the costs. For renters who cannot afford to move, advocates say those restrictions can leave few immediate options. 
Lily Coleman faced that dilemma when she and other residents at Addison Place Apartments in Jackson went more than a month without running water. 
Coleman, who has lived at the complex since 2018, said she continued paying rent because she did not want to risk eviction. 
“We’re going to still pay rent, and we are going to pay whatever we got to pay because we are not trying to get evicted,” Coleman said. “We don’t pay for the water over here — they pay for it.” 
 Coleman said the cost of moving also leaves her with few alternatives. 
“We cannot move right now,” Coleman said. “We’re trying to save some money right now to get in a position to move.” 
Several major water shutoffs at Jackson apartment complexes with large outstanding utility balances raised concerns about protections for tenants who can lose service because of bills tied to their properties.
Ashley Richardson, director of housing law at the Mississippi Center for Justice, said Mississippi’s Residential Landlord and Tenant Act needs reform. The Mississippi Legislature recently passed a law that makes it a crime to knowingly, willfully andunlawfully fail to apply utility payments collected from tenants to the bills for which the money was collected.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
Mississippi law strengthened those protections this year through House Bill 1404, which makes it a crime to knowingly, willfully and unlawfully fail to apply utility payments collected from tenants to the bills for which the money was collected. 
Ashley Richardson, director of housing law at the Mississippi Center for Justice, said the new utility law is progress but more is needed to protect tenants. 
The organization is seeking changes that include more notice before evictions for nonpayment of rent, regulation of rent-to-own housing contracts, changes to the repair-and-deduct law and creation of a state fair housing act.  
“In the work that I do with MCJ, I would say that the Mississippi landlord-tenant statute favors landlords more than tenants,” Richardson said. 
Rep. Fabian Nelson, a Democrat from Jackson. Credit: Mississippi Legislature
Mississippi’s Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires landlords to comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety and maintain rental units and their plumbing, heating and cooling systems in substantially the same condition as when the lease began, excluding reasonable wear and tear. 
Those requirements may not apply when a tenant deliberately or negligently causes the damage. State law also allows some maintenance responsibilities to be assigned through a written agreement. 
Tenants cannot simply stop paying rent when a landlord fails to make a repair. Instead, state law provides a process for making certain repairs and seeking reimbursement. 
To use that process, a tenant must provide written notice of a specific and material defect and give the landlord 30 days to make the repair. If the landlord does not, the tenant can pay for the repair and seek reimbursement.
After receiving receipts, the landlord has 45 days to reimburse the tenant or offset repair costs against future rent. 
Richardson said those requirements can make the process difficult when repairs are urgent or tenants cannot afford to pay upfront. 
“Depending on the repair, they might need something sooner than 30 days,” Richardson said. “A lot of the people that we service, they don’t have the money to pay for the repairs themselves.” 
Richardson said deposits and other upfront expenses can create similar barriers for tenants with limited financial resources. 
“We see that a lot of people don’t have the money to just pick up and move somewhere else,” Richardson said. 
Beyond the financial barriers, tenants can also struggle to understand what protections are available to them. 
Rep. Fabian Nelson, D-Jackson, has twice introduced legislation to loosen restrictions on the repair-and-deduct process. 
Nelson introduced bills in 2025 and 2026 that would have eliminated the one-month rent limit on repair costs and allowed tenants to use the remedy more than once in six months. His most recent proposal, House Bill 442, died in committee.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri charter school commission returns $685,000 in surplus funds to sponsored schools
description: Missouri’s largest charter-school sponsor entered August with nearly $3.3 million in its account, which is more than twice what it spent in the previous fiscal year. Now the Missouri Charter Public School Commission is sending some of that money back to the schools it oversees. At its August meeting, the commission approved $685,000 in rebates, […]
text:
Brookside Charter School in Kanas City is receiving $55,000 in a rebate from its sponsor the Missouri Charter Public School Commission (photo submitted).Missouri’s largest charter-school sponsor entered August with nearly $3.3 million in its account, which is more than twice what it spent in the previous fiscal year.
Now the Missouri Charter Public School Commission is sending some of that money back to the schools it oversees.
At its August meeting, the commission approved $685,000 in rebates, with individual schools receiving between $10,000 and $70,000. It is the third time in recent years the commission has returned a portion of its surplus to schools.
“Because we run a very lean but efficient agency, we are able to build up a healthy level of reserve,” Missouri Charter Public School Commission Executive Director Mark Modrcin told The Independent. “We feel like that should go right back to our schools, who could use those dollars better than we could.”
This funding, while a small portion of the cost required to run a school, can have a substantial impact on the school, several school administrators told The Independent.
Nicole Goodman, superintendent of Scuola Vita Nuova Charter School in northeast Kansas City, said the money goes a long way toward enriching students’ experience.
“There are things that keep us up at night when it comes to budgeting and knowing what the needs of our students and staff are,” she said. “It is really expensive to make sure we are giving all of our students the opportunities that they deserve.”
When she received word from the commission that her school would receive $70,000, she thought about field trips that she wanted to schedule but wasn’t quite sure the budget would allow for.
Goodman said the school tries to expose students to art, music, athletics and other activities without charging families fees for things such as instruments or field trips.
“There’s enrichment that we want to provide for our students and even our families to engage with their students more and to really truly be a partnership in this whole journey,” she said. “This helps us do a little more than we anticipated.”
For Brookside Charter School in Kansas City, extra funding fuels its growing operations. The school is set to open a second building in a year, and its $55,000 rebate will help make the transition run smoothly.
“The new building leads all of our conversations about the money that we have,” Superintendent Roger Offield said. “We’ve got to manage our dollars to do this.”
Offield doesn’t know exactly what the school will use the money for, but he anticipates that it will likely go toward staffing — which he says is paramount.
“Brookside’s philosophy has been that there’s no secret sauce to education. It is what quality adults do you put in front of kids,” he said.
The Missouri Charter Public School Commission is a state agency charged with providing oversight and accountability to charter schools. Local school districts and Missouri universities can also sponsor charters. To fund this task, state law dictates that charter sponsors receive 1.5% of their schools’ local and state aid, up to $125,000.
Sponsorship fees and federal grants have proven to be enough to sustain the commission’s operations. Last fiscal year, the commission spent over $1.4 million while taking in over $2.5 million, according to the State Treasurer’s annual fund report. And in July, the commission’s account had nearly $3.3 million.
During the meeting, commissioners briefly acknowledged that the $685,000 in rebates is just a portion of a healthy reserve balance. Finance committee chair Judith Meyer told the group that it would be nice to get media coverage but added, “We don’t want to talk too much about the amount of reserve that we have.”
State budget officials are predicting general revenue shortfalls in coming years and have instructed departments to limit future budget requests to only essentials. This frugality has placed extra pressure on education expenses, which make up a large chunk of the state budget.
But the commission’s large safety net is by design, Modrcin told The Independent.
“We have a policy where we keep reserves just in case something would happen to the state cash flow,” he said.
As for the rebates, the commission intends to be hands-off. The amount each school received was based on school size and performance, with the top-performing schools receiving $70,000 regardless of enrollment, but administrators will have discretion on how to spend the money.
On top of the $685,000 going directly to schools, the commission voted to put almost $95,000 in a grant program that will be administered by a third-party contractor. The details are not yet set, but the program is intended to fund ideas that foster better academic performance.
“We want to remember that we do not want to get involved in the management decisions of our schools,” Meyer said during the meeting. “We want that to come from the schools, but obviously in this case, we want them to focus on academic performance.”
Commissioners spoke about the grant program as an opportunity for schools to grow and share their successes for others to adopt.
“We’re grateful that we find ourselves in the position to be able to give back in this way to our schools,” Modrcin said. “And we hope that they put the money to good use.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri activists want fewer cameras on citizens and more on politicians
description: Pulaski County Sheriff Stacy Ball thinks Flock cameras help his deputies fight crime. But he also thinks they’re not worth keeping. Ball recently announced his office was pulling the plug on Flock Safety, the network of cameras that photographs license plates and gives police a database they can search later — and which has come […]
text:
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City (Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch).Pulaski County Sheriff Stacy Ball thinks Flock cameras help his deputies fight crime.
But he also thinks they’re not worth keeping.
Ball recently announced his office was pulling the plug on Flock Safety, the network of cameras that photographs license plates and gives police a database they can search later — and which has come increasingly under bipartisan fire across the country.
As far as Ball knows, his deputies never abused the system. He believes they used it responsibly. But he’s been hearing from residents worried about privacy, government surveillance and what could happen if the technology fell into the wrong hands.
In the end, that mattered more.
“Your voice matters. Your rights matter. Your trust matters,” he wrote.
Elsewhere in Missouri, the concerns of Flock critics aren’t hypothetical.
The St. Charles County Police Department shut down its network this month after discovering a civilian employee had used the database for a personal, non-law-enforcement purpose. The employee was put on unpaid leave and resigned after being notified the department intended to fire them. The misuse was uncovered after Flock rolled out a tool that flags unusual search patterns.
In Joplin, an officer left the department in January after an investigation found the system had been improperly used. Activists who reviewed the records said the officer accounted for roughly a quarter of the department’s Flock searches and ran one license plate about 395 times, typically listing “DWI” or “Warrants” as the reason without attaching a case number.
That helps explain why Flock has found plenty of skeptics in Missouri, especially among grassroots conservatives.
And they’ve picked up influential allies along the way.
“Americans do not surrender their privacy rights when they drive to work, drop their kids off at school, or go to church,” U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri said last week.
At the same time many of those conservatives are pushing back against Flock cameras in their communities, they’re demanding a camera be turned on in one particular place: the Missouri Senate.
For years, activists have wanted the Missouri Senate to livestream its proceedings. You can listen to the Senate online, but you can’t watch senators debate on the floor. It remains one of only two legislative chambers in the country where that’s true.
State Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, has repeatedly tried to change it. This spring, his proposal died in circumstances that would have been a little too on the nose if someone had written them into a screenplay.
Senators voted 12-11 to table Moon’s proposal using a standing division. That’s when senators physically rise from their desks to be counted, so there was no roll call showing who voted which way.
The Senate does record video of its proceedings, though, mostly for internal use. The conservative group Act for Missouri filed a Sunshine Law request, paid $6 and got a copy.
And at the point in the video when senators stood up to vote on whether Missourians should be able to watch the Senate, the screen went black.
Perfect.
Moon, as it happens, is also among a bipartisan group of lawmakers who sponsored legislation this year restricting state and local governments from using automated license plate readers.
The two positions may look contradictory, but the argument isn’t really over whether cameras are good or bad. It’s over on which side of the lens government belongs.
Police argue Flock cameras help them find stolen cars, missing people and suspects. But the cameras don’t wait until police suspect you of something. They photograph the cars that pass by and keep the information so police can search it later.
The Missouri Senate works the other way around.
These are elected officials conducting public business in a public building. Yet the Senate keeps video of that work largely for itself. If citizens want to see it, they have to ask, wait and sometimes pay for it.
Put the two fights next to each other and the politics make more sense. The government should have to justify watching you. You shouldn’t have to justify watching the government.
Maybe Missouri doesn’t have a camera problem.
Maybe the cameras are just pointed the wrong way.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: ‘Summery’ check in with voters
description: The Nebraska Legislature doesn’t convene for another four months, but a fresh look at what’s on voters’ minds is always helpful. That was clear at a recent legislative candidate forum in Lincoln. Six hopefuls shared the stage, answering questions primarily about environmental issues and then staying around to answer even more questions one-on-one. You know [[...]
text:
Data centers operate in Oregon in 2024. Some states are scaling back their data center incentives as the facilities contribute to increasing electric bills and raise environmental concerns. (Photo by Rian Dundon/Oregon Capital Chronicle)The Nebraska Legislature doesn’t convene for another four months, but a fresh look at what’s on voters’ minds is always helpful. That was clear at a recent legislative candidate forum in Lincoln.
Six hopefuls shared the stage, answering questions primarily about environmental issues and then staying around to answer even more questions one-on-one. You know … what they do in democracies.
That, plus you have to admire those who put themselves on the ballot these days, given the growing disdain throughout the precincts for government, politics and our institutions in general. So kudos to candidates Caitlin Knutson in District 2, incumbent Sen. George Dungan in District 26, former state Sen. Patty Pansing Brooks in District 28, Janet Bock in District 30, Shay Smith in District 32 and incumbent Sen. Danielle Conrad in District 46.
The evening was also a welcome respite from the miasma of our headlines: nonsense about renaming a Great Lake; further bad news on the inextricable quagmire with Iran; the increased cost of everything and now even more so if it has with a maple leaf stamped on it; measles deaths and explosive diarrhea; tainted meat and vaccine vagaries; and bad actors apparently hijacking the petition process in Nebraska. It’s exhausting.
The forum was a live, eyeball-to-eyeball affair, where each of the sextet acquitted themselves well on a variety of topics from clean energy to water quality to the consequences of climate change. These particular candidates — none of whom had their opponents on the dais with them — shared plenty of common ground. Still, it’s always instructive to hear personal perspectives, especially knowing from where they glean the information they use to develop a position or an opinion.
Whoever arrives at the Legislature the first week in January will be faced with a daunting task: addressing the 2027-2029 budget, which at this writing calls to mind images of the Red Sea as deficits approach the B-word. Thirteen of 49 senators will not be returning, whether via term limits or choice. That means in this election Nebraska voters have a chance to loosen the numerical headlock a supermajority can have on the legislative process.
The next Legislature will obviously be focused on extracting the state from its self-inflicted budget crisis. I’m guessing our annual head scratching over property taxes will fill a few days and weeks, too, but, if history serves — and it usually does — few will be satisfied with the outcome. Voting access, education and a myriad of other subjects will fill the chamber from Jan. 6, 2027, to about the first of June.
According to my reading of the candidates’ responses, two issues senators will be addressing next session emerged front and center at the forum: data centers and undoing the looting of the Environmental Trust Fund.
Apparently data centers, built to fuel the AI boom, are on the minds of many Nebraskans on whose doors the candidates have been knocking. They don’t want them. Government leaders, including in Nebraska, who had championed data centers to supply big tech its sustenance have also heard the ruckus opponents are making and slowed or backtracked incentives to bring the water-guzzling, power-sucking, heat-generating facilities to their neighborhoods.
Of course, the argument for data centers is that without them, we’ll fall behind in the AI race, an ill-defined contest that apparently will determine our future as a country or a species … something along those lines. On the way to securing this victory, we’re told, AI will make our lives more productive and efficient while simultaneously rendering many of our jobs obsolete.
That’s a lot to think about. Nebraska voters should demand their legislators do just that.
Finally, while a Lancaster County District judge has put a temporary kibosh on the process, no one among the candidates had anything remotely good to say about the recent budgetary practice of taking constitutionally protected money from the Environmental Trust Fund to essentially pay the state’s bills, using a sort of governmental procedural pass-through. A bill in the last session of the Legislature that would have put a constitutional amendment reaffirming the shielding of the trust’s funds on the ballot this November failed to advance. Is it just me or does it seem odd to have to amend the state constitution to say what it already says?
Not to belabor the point but to put the raiding of the trust’s money in apostolic proportions, Paul was depositing a check (ironically still not enough to cover his bills) while Peter was filing a police report for theft.
Meanwhile, early voting starts soon, so a glimpse about what’s on the minds of candidates — and voters — gives a fresh take on Nebraska’s axiom of citizen watchfulness.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Is a win a win among Oklahoma’s divided GOP electorate? Mike Mazzei is about to find out.
description: Congratulations and good luck to Mike Mazzei. He’s going to need it, as last week’s election results show. Mazzei won the Oklahoma GOP gubernatorial primary runoff by just over 2,000 votes.  A win may be a win, but in this case it should serve as a warning to both Mazzei’s campaign and the state Republican […]
text:
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, during his watch party in Tulsa, Okla. Mazzei secured the Republican nomination for Governor of Oklahoma by defeating Gentner Drummond.
(Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)Congratulations and good luck to Mike Mazzei.
He’s going to need it, as last week’s election results show. Mazzei won the Oklahoma GOP gubernatorial primary runoff by just over 2,000 votes. 
A win may be a win, but in this case it should serve as a warning to both Mazzei’s campaign and the state Republican party.
In 20 years of covering elections, I have never seen the outcome of a statewide race so close. The fact that it was reveals how fractured the Republican voting base really is, and that Mazzei will have a tough time getting the deeply divided rest of the state to coalesce behind his vision for our future. 
Heading into the primary election season, Mazzei took the traditionally conservative stance in highlighting that he believes human life begins at conception. He wants to eliminate Oklahoma’s income tax and abolish property taxes for veterans and senior citizens. And he wants expanded access to a tax credit program in which state taxpayers pay for wealthy families’ children to attend private school.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who lost in the primary runoff, laid out a more moderate path forward, with different priorities. 
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cyndi Munson put it best in a press release after polls closed on Aug. 25. Drummond, she said, campaigned on the issues we’re all facing — “struggling public schools, lack of access to healthcare, and rising costs of groceries, utility bills and other needs of everyday Oklahomans.” He wanted to invest more, not less in public schools.
It’s clear from last week’s election that Oklahomans are wondering if far-right policies – encapsulated by Mazzei – are serving us well.
The evidence says no.
Our rural hospital infrastructure is collapsing. A recent report found that 45 hospitals are at risk of closing — the third most in the nation.
We continue to have a mass exodus of quality educators. Even though our Legislature micromanages schools with mandatory recess time and high-stakes reading testing, we somehow don’t have the adequate policies — or compensation — that incentivizes teachers to remain. 
Access to mental health treatment is lagging, and we have some of the highest suicide rates in the nation.
We also have an exceptionally high poverty rate, which is straining our social service providers, our Medicaid system, and non-governmental nonprofits, like churches and food banks that have been forced to step in to fill the gap.   
Whoever wins in November’s general election will inherit this disaster that has progressively gotten worse under Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt the past eight years.
As the face of the GOP, Oklahoma’s over 1.2 million registered Republicans will be looking to Mazzei for a plan to fix this — and fast. And it better be a plan to solve the real issues because the tired tropes of attacking marginalized groups of people like trans kids and immigrants and fighting against abortion access are no longer unifying the Republican base.
Speaking of the base, you may be wondering where President Donald Trump fits into the picture for Oklahoma. He endorsed Mazzei ahead of the June primary election.
Mazzei made sure to thank the president for that during his election night victory speech. Unsurprisingly, he did not acknowledge why almost as many Republicans picked Drummond in spite of Trump’s endorsement.
Perhaps Mazzei’s supporters like Trump more than Mazzei’s plans.
Lawmakers would do well to remember that if the time comes to consider implementing Mazzei’s ideas. 
Trump may have the influence to be a kingmaker from the White House, but Oklahomans of all walks of life are living in a reality where Drummond’s platform spoke to them.
As Drummond said to Mazzei in his concession speech: “You have to show up for the farmers and ranchers. The small business owners and the working families. And you have to show up for the Oklahomans who didn’t vote for you.”
That includes, hundreds of thousands of registered independents who were locked out of weighing in on this race solely because they’re unaffiliated with any recognized political party, 
One last thing to consider: As Munson’s statement alluded, Democrats aren’t mad at the prospect of facing Mazzei in reliably red Oklahoma 
Their longshot odds of winning the governor’s office in November just went up a slight tick.
Mazzei’s GOP victory leaves open a crack in the door that Munson could take advantage of. To do that, she’ll need to figure out how to get Oklahoma voters to overlook the dreaded “Democrat” that will appear by her name.
That’s a tall order for anyone. But if Mazzei is unable to appeal to more moderate voters and develop a strategy to navigate our way out of our current morass, some voters may just hold their noses and vote for the Democrat come November. 
Or they might just stay home.
So, again, let me wish Mazzei luck over the next few months. 
He’s going to need it.
