name: Alabama Reflector
title: The danger for the Alabama GOP in the data center issue
description: There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to Fisher Ames, one of the first congressmen from Massachusetts. You can find different versions of it out there, but the idea is this. Monarchy is like a trim wooden sailing ship, with a captain delivering orders to officers who execute them without question. The vessel is a marvel, swiftly […]
text:
Residents of Lowndes County holding up signs that read "No Data Center" at a County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to Fisher Ames, one of the first congressmen from Massachusetts. You can find different versions of it out there, but the idea is this.
Monarchy is like a trim wooden sailing ship, with a captain delivering orders to officers who execute them without question. The vessel is a marvel, swiftly slicing the waves and turning with precision. But if it hits a rock, it sinks quickly.
Democracy is like a raft. It’s slow; it’s hard to maneuver, and your feet are always wet. But if it hits a rock, it stays afloat.
The Alabama Republican Party is neither clipper ship nor inflatable. It’s more of a wooden tub. Yet it’s gotten so used to favorable winds and calm water that it appears to be overlooking a major reef up ahead.
Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s insistence that data centers are good and their opponents are communist stooges hasn’t stopped the public outrage over the facilities. One data center proposed in Lowndes County — taking up 800 acres and reportedly using enough electricity to power 42% of all the homes in Alabama — drew at least 150 people to a county commission meeting last week.
Lowndes County isn’t alone. Across the state, local governments have tried to stop data center development or heard from large numbers of residents demanding they do so. Democrats have gotten behind gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones’ call for a yearlong moratorium on the facilities.
Tuberville, meanwhile, treats them as inevitabilities and makes dubious claims that they’ll be important revenue sources for their communities. Downballot Republicans may be trying to soften the blow, but in that deferential, whatever-you-say-boss manner that tells you where they’ll land.
After all, the Alabama politician is a creature who believes that “economic development” is magic that can take the place of governing (even though it probably doesn’t work). The Alabama politician ignores your concerns and tells you the real problem in Alabama is the fact corporations pay taxes in the first place.
That’s Alabama’s top-down approach to governing. Politicians believe they can tell voters what’s important. Zealots and lobbyists, in turn, can convince those officials that their weird or destructive obsessions are what matter.
Let’s be honest. If you ran into someone at a party loudly complaining about transgender people, they would come across as an obsessive and likely a creep. Yet a handful of bigots ensured that the GOP embraced obsessive creepiness in 2022 and 2024.
I want my children to learn American history with all its inspiration and tragedy. But a small group of brittle men in the Legislature not only made the teaching of a vague list of “divisive concepts” difficult but  gave schools like the University of Alabama an excuse to shut down spaces for Black and LGBTQ students.
Tuberville and other politicians bullied a Islamic school in Hoover and tried to make a controversy out of interfaith gatherings. With zero justification. And a spittle-drenched hatred straight out of Alabama’s Jim Crow era.
Did the public demand these attacks? Of course not. Ask Alabamians what they want from state government, and most will say a lottery or the end of the grocery tax.
Our grandees can’t deliver those. So they started telling voters in Alabama’s ever-lower turnout elections what they should care about. And it seemed to work.
No surprise, then, that the GOP’s gubernatorial nominee, cocooned in Alabama’s lickspittle conservative media, thinks he can order you to love data centers. If you don’t, he seems to assume that he can ignore the objections once elected.
And he’s probably right.
No other issue in recent years has better illustrated Alabama’s fundamental lack of democracy than data centers. County governments are often powerless to stop them because the state constitution denies them zoning authority (a point raised by both the Association of County Commissions of Alabama and the Lowndes County Commission). Even cities that have that authority are creatures of the Legislature. They may not want data centers, but anything they do – like setting a minimum wage – can be vetoed by lawmakers.
And the Alabama House and Senate? Dominated by Republicans, most of whom represent heavily gerrymandered, uncompetitive districts.
But despite all their institutional advantages, this is a genuine risk for Republicans.
Here is a broadly unpopular trend. Here are cities and counties rejecting the facilities. And here is a majority party that doesn’t see a problem.
Data centers will not turn Alabama purple. They will not magically transform Republicans into Democrats. What they could do is keep Republican voters home, a development the Alabama GOP can’t afford in a year where they face a clear enthusiasm gap. It’s possible screaming about socialism or Tuberville’s threats to subject Montgomery, a majority-Black city, to military occupation will draw some of those people to the polls. I wouldn’t count on it.
I’m not betting that Republicans will lose this fall. I’ve seen the great GOP ship steer confidently through trouble and over public opinion in the last 16 years. The data center issue may not be enough to sink it.
But the Republican captain is confident that it won’t. And he’s steering the vessel toward the rock.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tuberville, AG, GOP ask Alabama Supreme Court to affirm residency challenge dismissal
description: Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Thursday asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm a lower court’s dismissal of a case challenging his residency, with the backing of the state Attorney General’s Office and the Alabama Republican Party.  In a 62-page brief filed Thursday evening, attorneys for Tuberville called the plaintiffs’ appeal “prepos[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville on Thursday evening asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm the dismissal of a case challenging his residency. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Thursday asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm a lower court’s dismissal of a case challenging his residency, with the backing of the state Attorney General’s Office and the Alabama Republican Party. 
In a 62-page brief filed Thursday evening, attorneys for Tuberville called the plaintiffs’ appeal “preposterous,” writing that the Alabama Legislature has severely limited the courts’ abilities to hear election-related challenges under a law first passed in the 19th century.
“In truth though, there are multiple countervailing provisions of the Constitution that counsel against court action. To the extent that courts has a ‘special duty’ here because the Constitution is implicated, the duty extends to several other provisions,” the brief said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Messages seeking comment were left Friday with attorneys for the plaintiffs challenging Tuberville; Tuberville’s campaign and his legal team. 
The lawsuit argues that Tuberville does not meet Alabama’s seven-year residency requirement for the governorship. Tuberville has faced questions about his residency for years, and the plaintiffs’ complaint cites reporting including a homestead exemption in Auburn that Tuberville said he has been on since 2018 but was not added to until mid-2024, and a 2023 Florida driver’s license.
The case before the Supreme Court is not challenging Tuberville’s May primary win. It is seeking to allow the lower court to hear arguments about Tuberville’s residency.  
Tuberville has maintained that he meets the requirement, but does not deny that he owns a home on the Florida coast. In the Thursday brief, his lawyers argue that temporary absences do not strip a person’s resident status. 
“People that spend most of their time as agents of the state in Washington DC – like a U.S. Senator – would not lose their status as a ‘resident,’” it said. “Nor would they lose Alabama ‘resident’ status because they made regular visits to a Florida beach house they own or leave to go out of state on business every Sunday night to return on Friday night.”
His lawyers did not make it clear that Tuberville’s Auburn home – the listed address for his Senate candidacy, and often referred to as the “Game Day House” – is his primary residence. 
“Above all, (Section) 117 of the Constitution calls for the governor to be a ‘resident.’ In common parlance that probably means a shelter with a roof and walls that could be used as a place for sleep,” the brief said. “It does not obviously mean that being a ‘resident’ of some other place is forbidden. There is no adjective that disqualifies if the place is not a ‘primary residence.’”
The lawsuit made its way to the Alabama Supreme Court after Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hourslong hearing. Reid did not rule on the merits of the case. 
Does the Alabama Supreme Court have jurisdiction?
The Heflin-Torbert Judicial Building in downtown Montgomery, Alabama, seen on January 24, 2023. The building houses the Alabama Supreme Court and the state appellate courts. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and the Alabama Republican Party also submitted amicus briefs on Tuberville’s behalf on Thursday. 
Plaintiffs are seeking relief known as quo warranto, Latin for “by what authority,” challenging Tuberville’s right to hold office. Marshall argued that while courts do have jurisdiction over quo warranto cases and election challenges, the plaintiffs in this case erred in asking for it in this instance. He said that the case is a political issue, and it is up to the Legislature to resolve any election challenges.
“Courts have a vitally important role to play in many election disputes, but not this one,” he wrote in a 46-page brief.
Plaintiffs challenging Tuberville’s residency have argued that quo warranto it can be applied to party nominees like Tuberville as “quasi-officers” like Tuberville. Tuberville’s lawyers disagreed in Thursday’s brief.
“Alabama precedent rejects the conclusion that ‘quasi-officer’ status is sufficient to be challenged in a quo warranto action,” the brief said. 
Marshall wrote that Tuberville is only a public officer if he can perform the “sovereign functions” of the office, which he says the U.S. Senator cannot do as a gubernatorial nominee.
“A role defined by party governance and subordinate to party control is not a public office,” he wrote. “So the quo warranto statute, limited by its terms to public officers, does not extend to such party positions.”
During the lower court hearing, Tuberville’s lawyers asserted that the Alabama Republican Party and the Alabama Legislature have the authority to decide if the U.S. Senator meets the constitutional requirements for governor. The Alabama Republican Party dismissed a primary election challenge against Tuberville in June. 
In a Thursday afternoon brief, attorneys for the ALGOP argued that any further challenges should be dealt with by the Legislature.
“Moreover, the Legislature intentionally limited courts’ jurisdiction from hearing election disputes, instead granting the State’s political parties’ exclusive authority to settle their respective primary election contests,” the 31-page brief said.
Tuberville’s lawyers said the lawsuit is not “justiciable,” and nothing about that changes because the Legislature is a Republican supermajority.
“Changing the rules in the middle of an election is not good politics and sometimes becomes judicially actionable,” the brief said. 
Plaintiffs also requested oral arguments, but only if the justices have questions that are not answered in the briefs filed this month. Tuberville’s lawyers and Marshall objected to the request.
“There is no need to explore in oral argument the wisdom of an ‘extension’ of existing law. In the event this case cannot be resolved by summary disposition, it is likely moot, given the pace of the election process,” Tuberville’s brief said.
The Secretary of State certified all opposed state and federal candidates on Wednesday. The last day to withdraw from the ballot was Aug. 24. 
Tuberville’s lawyers also argued that the case is irrelevant because there can be no feasible relief at this point, since ballots are certified.
“As the debate is limited by the relators not to involve the elections, and no relief sought against any official that confers anything on Tuberville. Moreover, there is no person injured by Tuberville’s merely being a nominee,” the brief said. “Thus, in claiming they do not care that Tuberville won that election, they are the kind of litigants who merely want to debate, not resolve an injury in just fashion.”
The plaintiffs have one week to file a reply brief.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After two years of limbo, Kentucky’s kinship care is back on track
description: After two years of limbo, the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services has started implementing a 2024 law to help families who step in to raise a minor relative, known as kinship care families.  The Kentucky legislature approved and Gov. Andy Beshear signed SB 151 in 2024 to provide financial relief to grandparents and […]
text:
Michelle Tynes, of Hickory in Graves County, and her grandson, Ashton, are a kinship care family. An estimated 59,000 Kentucky children are being raised by relatives other than their parents. (Photo provided)After two years of limbo, the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services has started implementing a 2024 law to help families who step in to raise a minor relative, known as kinship care families. 
The Kentucky legislature approved and Gov. Andy Beshear signed SB 151 in 2024 to provide financial relief to grandparents and others who are raising children who otherwise would be in state care by making it easier for the family members to qualify for foster care payments.
Beshear’s administration contended that without specific funding — at one point, an estimated $20 million — it couldn’t implement the law. The General Assembly pushed back, saying he had the responsibility to implement it. 
For the next two years the legislature, auditor’s office and Beshear’s administration debated the issue — including in court — over who is responsible for funding the law and where the money should come from.
In Beshear’s budget request for 2026, he asked the legislature to appropriate $14.6 million in each fiscal year — nearly $30 million over the biennium — to fund the law. 
When the Senate initially added funds for SB 151 implementation, Beshear said “If they provide us $5 million, we’ll provide $5 million to those families.” 
By the end of the 2026 session, lawmakers upped the funding, giving Beshear $6 million each year — $12 million total — to fund SB 151. 
A July 15 letter from the cabinet to regional administrators and supervisors shared the Standard Operating Procedures for kinship care placements — essentially, guidance for cabinet employees on how to follow the law when considering placing a child in a kinship care home. 
Spokeswoman Beth Fisher said the cabinet had “authority” now to implement Senate Bill 151 thanks to language from this year’s House Bill 500, the two-year state budget. 
KY lawmakers increase money for kinship care in final budget 

“House Bill 500 contained language which gives the Dept. for Community Based Services (DCBS) the authority to implement Senate Bill 151 through its existing systems and processes,” Fisher said. “DCBS is using the funding it has access to that was included in the current state budget to support payments to eligible family caregivers.”
Norma Hatfield, a longtime kinship caregiver and advocate, has some concerns about the way the law is being implemented now — and what she sees as a lack of transparency around the new guidance. 
“When the funding came out, you had two years, you had a deficient regulation, and then you put a policy out there, it seems like quietly, without any public input,” she said. “Kinship caregivers deserve better. They — we — deserve a lot more than that. This thing should have been, to me, close to perfect after two and a half years, and that’s not what we got.” 
Hatfield has several main concerns about the policy as written, she said: 

“The placement decision process may be confusing and is tied to services and supports that differ depending on the path a caregiver takes. I feel that information about those options is not always consistent across the policy, forms, handbooks and public-facing materials, which can make it difficult for caregivers to make a fully informed decision.” 
“The qualifying-event application process — including the timeframes, notification methods and wording of the forms — may create unnecessary barriers for caregivers trying to access assistance.”  
“There are questions regarding Kentucky’s approach and about maximizing federal funds ensuring  protecting and supporting kinship caregivers.”   

She’s hoping for a full briefing with lawmakers and the cabinet to learn more about the full procedures to ensure potential kinship care families can both access help and do so without unnecessary confusion. 
In Late July, Fisher said the funds made available in the budget would go to relative and fictive kin foster parents receiving per diem for the children in their care. (Fictive kin are people who aren’t related to a child by blood or marriage but who have a strong connection with the child, such as a longtime family friend). 
Those payments depend on the age and needs of the child, according to Fisher. 

Basic is the primary payment for foster families when they start and ranges from $27 to $47 for medically complicated children. 
Advanced is a rate paid when foster parents have completed 2 years of fostering and 30 specific training hours. Payments for this range from $30 to $81. 


Care plus is a level of foster parenting that requires specialized training to care for youth with complex behavioral health needs. They require both initial and ongoing training hours. 


Medically complex requires specialized training, and the child must be deemed medically complex. 

“Team Kentucky believes every child should have a safe and loving home,” Fisher said, “and values the critical role of family caregivers in supporting children across our commonwealth.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Could Trump’s diminished popularity in Kentucky affect how this year’s midterm races are run?
description: President Donald Trump may no longer be the silver bullet in Kentucky elections that Republicans once had as voters face pains from an ongoing war in Iran and rising gas and grocery prices.  The president’s growing unpopularity in the Bluegrass may play into the central Kentucky 6th Congressional race in the weeks ahead as GOP […]
text:
Ralph Alvarado is the GOP candidate for the 6th District Congressional race in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Chris Hughes)President Donald Trump may no longer be the silver bullet in Kentucky elections that Republicans once had as voters face pains from an ongoing war in Iran and rising gas and grocery prices. 
The president’s growing unpopularity in the Bluegrass may play into the central Kentucky 6th Congressional race in the weeks ahead as GOP and Democrats hope to use their messaging to sway voters in a general election. 
Ralph Alvarado, the Republican nominee in the election, removed mentions of the president, who had endorsed him in the primary earlier this year, NBC News first reported Aug. 25. The changes included removing a photo of Alvarado and Trump from the homepage and referring to himself as a candidate for “independent leadership” when he once called himself an “America First fighter.”
As of Friday morning, the media page on Alvarado’s campaign site does still include a photo of the candidate and Trump. 
Months ago, Trump’s endorsements did well in Republican primaries. In Kentucky, Trump-backed Ed Gallrein defeated incumbent firebrand U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie in the 4th Congressional District by 10 points. Trump’s late-hour endorsements of Alvarado and U.S. Rep. Andy Barr in the Senate race led to both candidates sailing to comfortable leads in May. 
However, polling shows Trump’s approval underwater in many states, including states he has won in past elections like Kentucky. A YouGov/Economist projection released Aug. 21 showed the president’s job approval rating negative in all but three states. Kentucky was at -13 points in the findings. 
Reacting to the NBC story, the campaign for the Democratic nominee, Zach Dembo, said the move by Alvarado was an attempt “to try and paper over his real record” on the heels of a poll from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee saying Alvarado and Dembo are tied. DCCC has added the 6th District to its “Red to Blue” list, meaning it’s a priority race for funding and support. 
“If this is how Ralph treats his friends, imagine how quickly he will sell us out when it’s convenient,” Dembo said in a statement. “My opponent has proven he is just another two-faced politician who will say anything to try and get elected.”
Zach Dembo is the Democratic candidate for the 6th District Congressional race in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Chris Hughes)
Andy Westberry, a spokesman for Alvarado said in a statement the campaign has “proudly touted the endorsement” from the president and pointed to the photo of Trump and Alvarado on the site. 
“It’s no surprise this Biden alum is desperately trying to change the conversation,” Westberry said, referring to Dembo’s work as an attorney in the Justice Department during the Biden administration.
Morgan Eaves, the executive director of the Kentucky Democratic Party, said Trump’s lower approval rating is a reaction of voters to “the economic reality that is Trump’s America.” Since Trump began war in Iran, gas prices have gone up, increasing other costs like groceries.
“They’re being faced with the fact that, shockingly, it’s not popular to make those decisions, and so now you’re kind of seeing them play cleanup,” Eaves said of Republicans. “But voters aren’t stupid; they’ve already branded themselves. They’ve already made their views clear, and we’re going to continue to make sure voters don’t forget that.”
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Mike Ward, of Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, said Trump’s approval ratings are a “harbinger of the fall election.” Trump won the 6th Congressional District by 15 points in 2024, and if this “is a place where you have to downplay Trump, imagine the districts where he only won by five to 10 points,” Ward added. 
Kentucky Republicans are not so easily swayed. Adam Hope, the spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky, said the state is still a place Trump has won by 30-plus points and “he still has a pretty significant level of support.” Trump won Kentucky’s electoral votes in 2016, 2020 and 2024. 
“Polling is polling at the end of the day, but you look at the historical presence that the president has had in Kentucky, and that’s not going away anytime soon,” Hope said. RPK is continuing to see engaged GOP voters in Kentucky, as the party maintains a registration edge statewide and counties flip from Democrat to Republican. 
Still, Barr and U.S. Rep. James Comer – who have both tied their campaigns tightly to Trump – feel comfortable enough to address Trump’s new effort to bring down beef prices, something opposed by the Kentucky Cattlemen’s Association. On Thursday, Comer, who is the undeclared but early favorite GOP candidate for governor in 2027, said he has not been happy with Trump’s tariffs and their effects on Kentucky agriculture.
“I’ve expressed my displeasure with the president and the secretary of agriculture, explained why we don’t buy beef from Argentina,” Comer said. “And when you talk about America First, if we’re going to have tariffs — we should stick with it one way or the other.”
Barr’s campaign website has also shifted between the primary and general elections. According to Wayback Machine archives, the Barr website switched a photo on the homepage of Barr and Trump to one of Barr and two of his children in July. The wording also changed from “Kentucky Tough. 100% America First. Trump-Endorsed” to “Kentucky Tough, Kentucky First, Always.” As of Saturday, Barr’s homepage does note that the congressman was the first member of the Kentucky congressional delegation to endorse Trump and that he was the Kentucky chairman for Trump’s 2024 primary campaign.
Alex Bellizzi, a spokesman for Barr’s campaign, said “Kentuckians know that Andy Barr is proud to have President Trump’s endorsement” and the congressman “can’t wait to keep fighting for Kentucky alongside President Trump as our next U.S. Senator.”
Trey Grayson, a former Republican secretary of state, said “all good candidates pay attention to the political environment.” The array of voters candidates must reach in a closed primary election, with just members of their party, is different from a general election. As of July, independent and third-party voters make up about 12% of voters in the 6th District who will also be able to vote for Alvarado or Dembo for the first time. 
Grayson said one thing Republicans do have going for them this election cycle is that Democrats are still unpopular with voters. 
With how it is configured, the 6th District is still “a pretty good Republican district,” Grayson said. Anchored by Lexington, one of the state’s urban areas, it’s surrounded by rural counties. 
“He’s run before. He’s won before. He’s used to navigating some of this,” Grayson said of Alvarado. 
Kentucky’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky House Speaker says we should evaluate data center tax breaks. Let’s expand that idea.
description: Earlier this month, House Speaker David Osborne made an interesting comment to the Lexington Herald-Leader about whether Kentucky’s generous tax incentives to data centers were a good idea. “We should always be asking whether an incentive delivers a return for taxpayers, but we also need to make sure we’re comparing apples to apples before drawing […]
text:
Kentucky gives away about $9 billion in tax breaks every year. (Getty Images)Earlier this month, House Speaker David Osborne made an interesting comment to the Lexington Herald-Leader about whether Kentucky’s generous tax incentives to data centers were a good idea.
“We should always be asking whether an incentive delivers a return for taxpayers, but we also need to make sure we’re comparing apples to apples before drawing false conclusions disguised as economic analysis,” Osborne said. “Instead of looking at this in isolation, Kentucky has to evaluate these programs in the context of the broader economic development landscape.”
Despite the not very subtle dig at the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, which found that the legislature’s data center incentives could cost the state billions of dollars, Osborne was on to something. 
Kentucky gives away more than $9 billion a year in tax incentives, breaks and rebates, otherwise known as tax expenditures. By 2028, it will be nearly $10 billion. Do they work in the “broader economic development landscape?” 
We don’t know because we don’t “evaluate” them.
But we love to hand them out. We give them to gigantic replicas of Noah’s Ark, we use them to evict mobile home park residents, we give them to millionaire horse owners, fancy shopping malls, ostrich farmers, Hallmark movie directors and much, much more.
You can read all about them in the Tax Expenditure Analysis, a handy report written every year by the Office of State Budget Director. 
Now there are some big ones, like a sales tax break on food and medications, that probably help people. But a lot of these are corporate welfare, plain and simple, and they are often awarded not on merit but on the size of their lobbyists’ delegation. (It helps if the lobbyists are former legislators.)
Once, someone did do something. Or tried. Louisville Republican Rep. Ken Fleming, chaired a task force that concluded Kentucky should keep the top 10 most expensive tax expenditures, like food and medicine, and get rid of the rest. 
Did his colleagues jump at this chance to save money? Not a bit, even though they are now trying to eliminate the state income tax. It would take some brave politicians to stand up to the herdsmen of all those sacred cows.
But maybe Rep. Osborne is ready. Given the statewide outrage over data centers, one of his colleagues hinted the General Assembly might be making some changes to the generous incentives offered to data center developers.
And the aforementioned Kentucky Center for Economic Policy has also pointed out that depending on how data centers are classified – “manufacturing” or “industrial processing” facilities – they could possibly qualify for more breaks in local property taxes or sales taxes on energy costs, which already exist.
Data centers have provoked some deep vein of bipartisan anxiety in Kentucky, ostensibly about pollution and high costs, but more viscerally centered around AI, children and social media, job loss, and fears of being controlled by feckless tech bros. Politicians from both parties, including Gov. Beshear, now say if data centers are so great, they should pay their own  way. 
But while we’re at it, why don’t we see how much good all those other tax giveaways are doing for our economy. It’s exciting that Osborne agrees, and maybe with his political heft, Kentucky could finally see if all these giveaways make any sense.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia health leaders, lawmakers share enhanced healthcare resources for rural communities
description: Eastern Shore residents and healthcare providers on Friday told state leaders about the opportunities and challenges they face serving their communities, with Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa outlining how the state government can support them and other rural Virginians.  “We’re here to learn what the challenges are, what the[...]
text:
Eastern Shore Rural Health CEO Jeanette Edwards shows Virginia Health and Human Resources Secretary Marvin Figeuroa a radiology room at the organization's Eastville clinic on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Eastern Shore residents and healthcare providers on Friday told state leaders about the opportunities and challenges they face serving their communities, with Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa outlining how the state government can support them and other rural Virginians. 
“We’re here to learn what the challenges are, what the assets are and ‘how (we can) scale the work,” Figueroa  said at Eastern Shore Community College, one of several stops on the listening tour. 
The same day, the  state announced $122 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund awards were disbursed to healthcare organizations around the state. Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin applied for the new federal grant last year.
The next RHTF funding wave will be allocated by the end of October, and Virginia has $189 million total to spend over time. Figueroa and his team are responsible for distributing the funding and coordinating with Gov. Abigail Spanberger and state lawmakers on its use. 
Del. Rob Bloxom, R-Accomack, joined Figueroa for the multi-stop tour, which highlighted the regional workforce and the unique connection they have with the people they serve. The local community college, the Eastern Shore Area Agency on Aging, Riverside Shore Memorial Hospital, local health centers and various nonprofits participated. 
Juan Gomez, an outreach coordinator with Eastern Shore Rural Health — a set of regional federally qualified health centers — described part of his work helping people  sign up for health insurance at public events. 
One of the clinic’s licensed practical nurses, Nicole Crockett, is an Eastern Shore native and has been with the clinic for 13 years. 
“People know my face and feel comfortable because of that,” she said. 
With her focus on pediatrics, she’s enjoyed watching the children she cares for grow up. To level up her career, she is also taking courses at the Eastern Shore Community College for a Registered Nurse degree. 
Of the clinics’ over 400 employees, CEO Jeanette Edwards said that about half of them have graduated from the local college or are pursuing additional degrees or certifications there. 
The day’s dialogue broached the looming changes stemming from H.R.1, the reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer that’s expected to trigger loss of Medicare and other healthcare benefits for millions nationwide. 
The impact may be felt unequally in the state and hit rural areas hard, Bloxom said.  
“When you go around rural parts of Virginia, not everyone has the network of people like we do. But we have things to worry about and we need to adjust,” Bloxom said. 
Because of the new standards, Figueroa said, “We’re losing more than we’re getting.”
The RHTF money can boost services at clinics, hospitals and nonprofits, and strengthen staffing, telehealth and workforce development, Figueroa added. 
The state is also bracing for eligibility and procedural changes to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
Of Virginia’s two million Medicaid enrollees, about 300,000 are at risk of losing their insurance, while about 5,800 lawful immigrants will lose their eligibility for it. Roughly 749,000 Virginians are also SNAP recipients. 
Additionally, Congress let Affordable Care Act subsidies expire, leading thousands of Virginians to drop that form of insurance due to higher premiums. 
Virginia’s latest budget earmarked $150 million for a state-level version of the ACA subsidy that will be available this fall. The money will also provide a funding boost for federally qualified health centers and free clinics. 
Hospitals are also expected to grapple with a forthcoming change in funding mechanisms it uses to help support Virginia’s Medicaid expansion. The various forthcoming cuts paired with long-established rural healthcare challenges means that 13 rural hospitals are at risk of service cuts or closure, a state report found. 
Last week Spanberger signed an executive order to solidify state and local government directives to streamline H.R. 1 implementation efforts. 
“It’s a new system to build” before the changes kick in Jan. 1, Figueroa said. 
The  state has created plain language toolkits for announcement materials that local agencies and nonprofits can use to make signs and handouts, Figueroa said, to help residents determine if they’re eligible and understand how to navigate the new process.
Even with streamlining efforts by state and local agencies, the event’s attendees said they were concerned that people may lose their benefits due to challenges in their own lives amid the new, twice-yearly verification requirements and eligibility standards. 
Northampton department of social services worker Mozella Francis said that she encounters many Medicaid or SNAP beneficiaries that lack consistent phone or computer access. Others may not have a car or easy access to public transit. 
Francis implored Bloxom and his counterparts in the state legislature to do more to address transportation hurdles in rural areas. 
Throughout the day, Figueroa reiterated the “tough time” patients, providers and public servants will have ahead of them. He noted the “bond” he feels with residents and healthcare workers around the state and said he is “committed” to helping ensure people can navigate the changes as smoothly as possible. 
“We can’t solve all of people’s life problems but it’s our responsibility to not make it worse,” he said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia voters to decide on 1% sales tax for school construction, NoVa transit funding
description: Voters in 47 Virginia jurisdictions will weigh a 1% sales tax to fund school construction and modernization costs. In Northern Virginia, the revenue could also support transportation projects. This comes as leaders face funding challenges for aging school facilities and rising demand to support Metro and other local transit systems.  Before the tax is implem[...]
text:
A 2021 tour of the construction of the new Highland Springs High School in Henrico. This fall, voters in several localities will decide whether to impose a 1% sales tax to fund school construction and modernization costs. (Photo courtesy of Henrico County Public Schools)Voters in 47 Virginia jurisdictions will weigh a 1% sales tax to fund school construction and modernization costs. In Northern Virginia, the revenue could also support transportation projects.
This comes as leaders face funding challenges for aging school facilities and rising demand to support Metro and other local transit systems. 
Before the tax is implemented in each locality, residents must vote in favor of the measure in November. The option was extended to all jurisdictions after this year’s legislative session, following years of debate in the General Assembly about expanding the authority.
“It’s been a long journey, but it’s rewarding to see it finally get across the finish line, and to see that so many folks want to use this to help their communities,” said Jeremy Bennett, director of intergovernmental affairs for the Virginia Association of Counties.
Josette Bulova, policy communications coordinator for the Virginia Municipal League, said 13 of the league’s 39 members have added the question to their respective ballots.
“Having this other continuous funding source is really helpful to everybody,” Bulova said.
About 58% of Virginia’s counties and cities are not seeking any change.

Bennett and Bulova said some localities held back because they didn’t need the authority right now, it didn’t solve their capital or revenue problem, or they preferred to wait for a future year.
“It might be a really good choice for some localities, but it might not be a good fit for others,” Bennett said.
Select registered voters can vote early on the ballot question beginning on Sept. 18 through Oct. 31, or by mail. The deadline for the Nov. 3 election is 5 p.m. on Oct. 23. Returned absentee ballots generally must be postmarked by Election Day and received by the local registrar by noon on the third day after the election.
After a four-year hiatus, the Commission on School and Modernization will meet on Sept. 8. Virginia passed legislation extending the commission, which was set to expire on July 1.
The law now eliminates the expiration date on the commission and it directs the group to meet at least four times each year. 
 New tool eases tax burdens

For many localities, Bulova said the appeal of the new sales tax is that it creates a dedicated, continuous revenue stream for school construction without levying more real estate taxes on residents. 
She pointed out that local governments have “not a lot of ways to raise revenues for schools specifically,” and that most of the burden has traditionally fallen on property owners at a time when the cost of living is already high. 
A local sales tax, she said, spreads the cost more broadly — including to visitors and commuters who shop in a community — rather than placing the full weight of school construction on residents’ property tax bills.
Since 2019, interest in finding an alternative revenue source to fund aging school facilities has grown, backed by legislative efforts, facility tours, and a 2021 Virginia Department of Education survey that found more than half of the state’s schools are over 50 years old. Replacement costs are in the billions.
Meanwhile, Northern Virginia leaders are facing rising costs to support Metro and local transit systems. Leaders urged lawmakers to provide additional funding on top of its regular appropriation.
 How the new funding tool came to be

Virginia is a “Dillon’s Rule” state, which means local governments can only exercise powers granted by the state legislature. Localities can adjust property tax rates, but they need General Assembly approval to change sales taxes.
In 2019, Halifax County became the first locality to receive authority. Now, the list has grown to nine localities: the city of Danville and the counties of Charlotte, Gloucester, Henry, Mecklenburg, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania.
Lawmakers have attempted to expand the authority, but have either failed in the General Assembly or been vetoed by former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, citing concerns about adding to Virginians’ tax burden and highlighting that millions of dollars were appropriated for school construction.
Schools get modernization grants
On Thursday, the Virginia Board of Education approved $577 million in grants to schools across the commonwealth. The average project cost for award recipients was $16.98 million, according to the VDOE’s fiscal year 2026 School Construction Assistance Program award document.
The city of Virginia Beach had the most expensive project at $100 million to construct a new Princess Anne High School building, expected in 2028. The city of Winchester also received an award for its $86.9 million renovation and expansion project for Garland Quarles Elementary.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Public utilities shouldn’t be funding the campaigns of the people who govern them
description: Virginia House Speaker Don Scott is adamant that the nearly $4 million in campaign funds he has accepted from Dominion Energy won’t affect how he views the Virginia utility’s attempt to merge with Florida-based NextEra.  Scott reportedly told a Virginia Public Radio reporter last week, “If you can’t take their money, eat their food and […]
text:
"This year," as lawmakers and regulators weigh the proposed $67 billion Dominion Energy-NextEra mega merger, "the need for reform is especially urgent," columnist Ivy Main writes. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia House Speaker Don Scott is adamant that the nearly $4 million in campaign funds he has accepted from Dominion Energy won’t affect how he views the Virginia utility’s attempt to merge with Florida-based NextEra. 
Scott reportedly told a Virginia Public Radio reporter last week, “If you can’t take their money, eat their food and tell them no, then you need to go home.” 
Scott is, by all accounts, a very smart man, but I just have to ask: is he kidding himself, or us? 
I can’t answer for the Speaker, but I think I have enough of a grasp of human nature to know that what he is saying is bunk. 
If someone gives you something – even if it goes to your political campaign and not into your pocket directly – it influences you. It has to. Humans are hard-wired for this. Giving and taking – cooperating with each other – is at the root of our success as a species.
SCC commissioner, former NextEra attorney declines to recuse herself from merger case

It’s why government ethics laws, including Virginia’s, have broad prohibitions on their employees accepting gifts that might influence them in doing their jobs. (Politicians have different rules.)  
No doubt some of us are more susceptible than others. Me, for example. Offer me something as trifling as a $3 item of corporate swag, and my feelings about you will grow a little warmer and fuzzier. Give me produce from your garden, and I am your friend for life. I know quite well that if I were to lose my mind and run for office, the only thing that would save my honor is my innate suspicion of anyone who tells me I’m great. 
Many legislators I have talked to who take Dominion money believe themselves to be made of sterner stuff. Money, flattery – they figure they can accept it as their due and never give anything back. Not a one of them admits to being influenced. If you point out that their committee votes align with Dominion’s interests more often than not, they will insist it’s because Dominion’s lobbyists are so good at what they do. 
I wonder how many voters buy that argument. I suspect they look at campaigns awash in corporate cash and feel only disappointment in their leaders, or cynicism about government altogether. 
Virginia is one of only five states that allow unlimited corporate donations to the campaigns of elected officials. Until just this year, shockingly, it didn’t even bar those officials from using their campaign money for personal expenses. (Florida, the home state of NextEra, limits contributions to candidates for legislative office in any election to just $3,000.) 
Defenders of Virginia’s status quo argue that there’s no harm as long as candidates disclose the donations, giving constituents the chance to vote out legislators if they are sufficiently outraged. Dominion hedges against this unlikely outcome by contributing to members of both parties. 
In any event, retribution is unlikely. Former Del. Tim Hugo, excoriated in the Washington Post back in 2013 for using campaign funds to pay a $9,000 personal cell phone bill, nonetheless sailed to reelection that fall. Hugo didn’t lose his seat until the 2019 “blue wave” election shifted his district to Democratic. 
Indeed, our campaign laws feel like a relic of the Old South’s reverence for personal honor. It’s as though adding limits would impugn the integrity of the gentlefolk who selflessly serve the public. 
According to the same nostalgic fantasy, campaign contributions are akin to philanthropy. In that bygone world that never existed, a corporation like Dominion would choose the recipients of its largesse based not on who can be expected to vote in its favor, but according to who it believes most capable of making laws benefitting the public.
But Dominion is not running a charity. It would not spend millions of dollars on legislators’ campaigns if it did not expect a return on its investment. Moreover, if donations did not produce the expected benefits, the company would stop making them. In the cold calculus of the real world, political spending equals influence equals profits. 
Dominion is also not concerned with ensuring that only smart, civic-minded people get into office. It confines its campaign spending to lawmakers who are already in office, with most of the money going to those in leadership positions or who are on the committees that have the greatest power to affect its bottom line. 
If giving money to campaigns did not make the company richer, you would expect Dominion to welcome campaign finance reform measures outlawing donations from public utilities. Prohibiting those donations would save the company tens of millions of dollars every year. 
But Dominion opposes the reform bills. The company claims its participation in “the political process” is on behalf of its employees and customers; it makes no mention of its shareholders.
Dominion’s lobbyists say the company favors a comprehensive approach to reform that addresses all donations, rather than singling out public utilities. Meaning, it won’t support this bill, but it might be okay with a different one that – oh, too bad! – has less chance of passing. Meanwhile, it intends to keep its favored legislators on its dole.  
Virginia’s loose campaign finance laws have survived years of reform efforts that came from members of both parties, only to be killed on orders of both parties’ leaders. But the Democratic Party of Virginia has stopped accepting money from Dominion, and today, most rank-and-file Democrats eschew donations from utilities. 
This puts Scott and several other leaders at odds with those they lead. With a Democratic trifecta now, there’s a golden opportunity for the party to prove to voters that it cares more about their interests than its own. 
This year, the need for reform is especially urgent. If NextEra acquires Dominion to become the nation’s largest utility without the General Assembly acting to limit campaign spending, nothing will stop NextEra from flooding campaigns with so much cash that all pretense of legislators’ independence will be lost. 
That shouldn’t be acceptable to anyone.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Thousands of signatures put a question on Providence’s November ballot. One country is the target.
description: Dave Talan thinks it’s hateful. Rep. David Morales thinks it’s the right thing to do. And Providence Mayor Brett Smiley thinks it’s legally unenforceable. The candidates in Providence’s mayoral race are divided over Question 7, a citizen-led proposal that will appear before Providence voters on the Nov. 3 ballot. The ordinance — buoyed by two […]
text:
Providence Republican mayoral candidate Dave Talan speaks with a woman outside Bell Street Chapel on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, before a mayoral forum. Talan, a board member of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel, joined the group’s rally against Question 7, a divestment proposal on the November ballot. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Dave Talan thinks it’s hateful. Rep. David Morales thinks it’s the right thing to do. And Providence Mayor Brett Smiley thinks it’s legally unenforceable. 
The candidates in Providence’s mayoral race are divided over Question 7, a citizen-led proposal that will appear before Providence voters on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The ordinance — buoyed by two rounds of petitions, thousands upon thousands of signatures, and a seldom-used provision of the city charter — would limit city investments when they are tied to foreign countries “conducting severe violations of human rights such as ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.”
Israel is not named in the proposed ordinance, but the country’s actions against Palestinians are at the crux of the campaign for its passage. 
Morales, a democratic socialist challenging Smiley in the primary, joined the mayor and Talan, the race’s lone Republican, at Bell Street Chapel on Federal Hill on Aug. 25, where a mayoral forum outlined the candidates’ differences.
Outside the Unitarian Universalist church, the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel had organized a modest rally against the measure to coincide with the forum. 
“It’s absolutely targeted right at Israel,” Ken Schneider, president of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel, said of the proposal, holding a massive banner with the group’s name and website in his hand. “Even though it doesn’t even say the word Israel in the ballot question, it’s all about Israel.”
Should the measure pass, Schneider added, “We think it would hurt Israel. We think it would hurt Jews.”
Talan joined the coalition members lingering outside the church who, Schneider said, were mainly there to educate voters about Question 7, rather than tell voters which candidate to support. Talan sits on the coalition’s board and calls the measure a case of “open antisemitism” that would cost the city’s pension fund millions.
“It would make the 15,000 Jewish residents in our community feel uncomfortable,” Talan wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current. “And it would send a terrible message to anyone thinking of investing in Providence.” 
At the forum inside the chapel, Talan castigated the measure, as well as Morales’ support for it. Morales, meanwhile, defended Question 7 to loud applause and a few boos. Smiley got some applause of his own when he argued the measure would conflict with the city charter.
Smiley, who converted to Judaism in 2024, called the measure “another moment that’s going to create division and sow division within our community.”
The Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island is opposing Question 7, according to a statement from its president and CEO Steven A. Baker. 
“Like many of our neighbors in Providence, we have concerns about how this proposed measure would impact the health of Providence’s pension fund and the financial well-being of our public safety and municipal retirees,” Baker wrote.
Over 6,000 verified signatures collected
The effort to get the divestment question before voters took a united front: Providence for Palestine, the coalition behind the divestment proposal, comprises an assortment of progressive groups — Jewish Voice for Peace Rhode Island, Reclaim Rhode Island, the Rhode Island Democratic Socialists of America and AFT Local 6516, the Brown University higher education workers’ union. 
Under Section 209 of the city charter, Providence residents can petition for a city ordinance with the weight of at least 1,000 signatures from qualified voters behind them. Organizers cleared that benchmark with 1,005 signatures, according to City Clerk Tina Mastroianni. Those signatures were received by the City Council on April 16, which was then charged with acting on the proposal.
The council didn’t enact the proposal, so ordinance supporters had to get signatures from an additional 5% of Providence’s qualified voters. Organizers needed a total of 5,549 signatures, and 6,036 were ultimately verified and qualified, Mastroianni said.
Providence for Palestine organizer Adit Sabnis said in a phone interview that the signature-collecting effort began modestly at first, with 20 to 30 people beginning to circulate the petition around February and March this year. 
The goal was simple. “Just talking to as many people as possible,” Sabnis said.
“We would go out to different events where there were things happening,” Sabnis added. “Sometimes we’d just go around, walk around neighborhoods. Sometimes we’d say ‘OK, does anyone want to chill at the pedestrian bridge at 7 p.m.?’”
As the months stretched into summer, more than 100 people had joined the effort, Sabnis said, and “people were bringing their friends in” to help collect signatures. Volunteers worked neighborhood happenings and public events, with campaign-related outings serving as valuable venues once election season intensified with mayoral debates and forums spreading across the city.
Members of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel, including board member and Republican candidate for Providence mayor Dave Talan, seen at right, rally outside Bell Street Chapel in Providence on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, ahead of a mayoral forum. The group opposes Question 7, a divestment proposal that both opponents and proponents argue targets Israel, despite the country never being named in the ordinance. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
The organization collected more than 10,000 signatures, Sabnis said.
“Honestly, we were shocked — not shocked, but we were overwhelmed by how receptive and happy people were to see us doing this,” Sabnis said. “So it was really, really validating to see.”
Why did organizers turn to the oft-neglected Section 209, rather than more traditional means of persuading elected officials via lobbying or advocacy pressure?
“So many times, the leaders and politicians that we try and lobby have other interests at heart, and it almost feels like a futile effort,” Sabnis said. “I really like the idea of us reclaiming our power in the sense that we’re no longer going and begging politicians to do what’s right by their constituents. We’re taking it into our own hands.”
Such petitions are unusual in Providence but not unheard of. Mastroianni pointed to a 2014 effort which predated her time in the office and would have established a minimum wage for hotel workers. It had enough signatures and won approval with a council resolution, but it never reached the ballot.
The year after that, Mastroianni added, residents tried to establish another ballot question, this time over public funding for stadiums, but it was halted because it involved an appropriation of money — something specifically excluded from Section 209’s permissions, per a city Law Department memo at the time.
‘Expertly written’
Broadly speaking, divestment is a strategy for disentangling from institutional investments in companies, industries or governments which an investor no longer wants to support. The ordinance underlying Question 7 would limit the city’s investment in entities involved in genocide and other violations of human rights. 
The proposed ordinance defines companies “complicit” in these violations if they “directly and knowingly enable and contribute” to such abuses. Under the ordinance, direct investments in eligible companies would cease, and the city treasurer would review the municipal portfolio annually for compliance.
Most of Providence’s pension money, however, is not invested directly in individual companies or countries, a May 2026 investment report shows.
Per the report’s numbers, the city’s pension fund was valued at about $636.3 million as of May 31, its monies spread across an array of external managers, index funds and other investment strategies. 
Among the holdings were $241.1 million managed through a State Street Russell 1000 strategy, $42.3 million in a Fidelity international index fund and $8.2 million in Vanguard’s Total International Bond Fund. 
During a similar divestment debate in 2024, Providence officials had said that the city held no State of Israel Bonds directly, but that the then-$7.5 million invested in the Vanguard bond fund held about $30,000 in Israeli bonds. 
The Brown Daily Herald reported then that the city still held a little over $2.3 million in Israeli bonds in 2021, but that these matured in 2022 and were not reinvested. 
The proposed ordinance would treat these indirect investments differently from securities held directly by the city. 
“If the city has or plans to invest indirectly in either co-mingled accounts or state-managed funds, it will officially and publicly ask the managers of these accounts or funds to consider adopting the above restrictions on its investments,” the ordinance reads.



Quotation







I really like the idea of us reclaiming our power in the sense that we’re no longer going and begging politicians to do what’s right by their constituents. We’re taking it into our own hands. 


– Providence for Palestine organizer Adit Sabnis 


Salar Ghahramani, a professor of business law and international law at Penn State University who studies public pension divestment mandates, said outside management does not always mean an investor is unable to fulfill divestment obligations.
“They would simply ask the external managers…to shift the existing investments and to change the existing contract that the city has to another investment strategy or portfolio that the external manager offers, in order to remain compliant with the initiative,” Ghahramani said. 
Ghahramani cautioned, however, that existing contracts may not always allow immediate flexibility, and investments can be subject to certain time-bound terms. That could prevent the city from shifting money around before a certain date, Ghahramani said, although he was not privy to the specific terms of Providence’s investments.
Carl Austin Miller Grondin, a spokesperson for the mayor’s office, said that the ordinance “contains broad and conflicting provisions regarding direct and indirect investments, while expressly recognizing the City’s existing fiduciary responsibilities.”
Miller Grondin also cited a state law that “establishes fiduciary obligations that govern the management of City funds,” but did not point to a specific law. 
Vanguard, which managed the international index fund for Providence in 2024, did not respond to inquiries about its practice or policies regarding investors who need to divest from specific companies or countries.
As for the protections the ordinance affords the city’s pension fund, Ghahramani said fiduciary duties of trustees involve two components: “the maximization of the returns for the beneficiaries,” but also abiding in the law. 
When it comes to fulfilling these fiduciary duties, Ghahramani said, “Breaking the law to maximize returns for the beneficiaries would be a hard sell.” 
What stood out most to the professor, however, was the way in which the ordinance was “expertly written.” 
Generally, divestment policies have been at the state level and target particular countries, Ghahramani said, but Providence’s Question 7 relies on a broader definition rooted in international treaties and, also uncommon, a notion of “complicity.” 
While other examples of this treaty-based wording may exist, Providence’s divestment measure is the only one Ghahramani said he has encountered. He noted the Supremacy Clause in Article VI of the U.S. Constitution, which establishes the Constitution, federal law and U.S. treaties as “the supreme Law of the Land.” Ghahramani thought Question 7 “implicitly yet expertly incorporates” that principle by relying on treaties in which the U.S. is a party.
Whether Providence could make those changes and leave its portfolio’s performance unscathed is unclear. Miller Grondin said the city’s Law Department has concluded that Question 7 cannot lawfully direct or restrict Providence’s current investment decisions, because the Board of Investment Commissioners is the only body with the authority to make investment decisions under the city charter. 
Attorneys for the Jewish Alliance made similar arguments in a July 21 letter to the city, contending that it could “create an inherent irreconcilable conflict” with the city’s fiduciary obligations to its pensioners.
The financial effects of the proposal depend on the particular restrictions attached to a portfolio, Clair Brown, an economics professor emerita at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies public pension divestment and fiduciary duty, said in an email. 
Brown’s research has focused on divestment from fossil fuels rather than countries accused of human rights violations. But at least in the pension systems she studied, Brown said her research showed that “risk must be part of fiduciary duty,” and that fossil fuel divestment was a “prudent” choice within that set of obligations. 
Still, Brown cautioned that individual scrutiny is needed to ascertain the effects of a particular divestment. Generally, the more companies a divestment policy excludes, Brown said, the more it can limit a portfolio’s ability to balance risks and expected returns.
Providence mayoral candidates participate in a forum at Bell Street Chapel in Providence on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Targeting Israel and future violators
Whatever the ultimate financial effects, supporters and opponents alike agree that the campaign is going after one country in particular.
“Israel is one of the primary targets now because of their genocide in Palestine,” Sabnis said, and added that it was written to accommodate future violators as well. “It’s something that we hope will set us up for the long term, so that we don’t have to keep having this conversation.”




Quotation







Even though it doesn’t even say the word Israel in the ballot question, it’s all about Israel. 


– Ken Schneider, president of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel


From the other side’s perspective, the divestment question is “antisemitic” and “illegal and unenforceable,” Talan said in an email ahead of the rally and forum Tuesday. The mayoral candidate said he would resist implementing the ordinance even if Providence voters approve it.
“I will instruct all city financial people to ignore it, and dare the pro-Palestinian sponsors to challenge me in court,” Talan said. 
When a question about the proposal came up at Tuesday’s forum, Morales defended it, saying that he’s heard from residents an unwillingness to “see any form of public investment or public taxpayer dollars…going towards genocide or rights of humans being violated overseas.” 
“I think we have a moral responsibility to speak out when injustices are happening, and recognize that even here at the local level, we have a responsibility…And the way in which the ordinance is written is very thoughtful in terms of the approach on how we ensure that it is compliant on a legal basis.”
Loud applause followed Morales’ answer, along with a few boos mixed in.
An email ahead of the forum from Ben Shanahan, Morales’ campaign manager, said legal or implementation questions should not be used “as a reason to disregard the will of the voters,” and that the divestment proposal already includes “language intended to avoid some of the legal criticisms raised against it, such as a severability clause and considerations of fiduciary duties.” 
Smiley, meanwhile, had previously expressed his opposition to the measure and remained opposed Tuesday night. He told the packed room that the proposal would conflict with the city charter, and he said that the city’s treasurer had also deemed it unenforceable. 
Outside the church, before the forum, the Israel coalition’s Schneider predicted litigation in the city’s future.
“There’s lawyers that are lined up,” Schneider said, pointing to legal disputes in Pittsburgh and Somerville, Massachusetts, over comparable divestment measures.
The Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island did not respond to a question about whether it would take legal action. Baker said the alliance plans to work with partners throughout Providence leading up to November’s general election in hopes of educating voters about the potential financial consequences of approving Question 7, as well as “the message of division and potential exclusion this ballot measure sends to the Jewish community.”
Providence for Palestine will also campaign for the measure’s passage, with special attention on the primary, “because we know so much of our ability to enforce it is also dependent on having allies [on the City Council],” Sabnis said. 
Sabnis said he was encouraged about the ballot question’s prospects, given the alliance’s success in securing the signatures Question 7 needed to exist in the first place. He mentioned organizers who approached people to sign the petition only to be told no. The reason? 
“‘I already signed this. I already signed this. I already signed this,’” Sabnis recalled hearing. “We’re like, ‘Dang, we have that much reach.’”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island bought the Flock cameras. It forgot to write the rules.
description: I spent 20 years as a police officer, commanded the Investigative Services Division, and worked a federal drug task force alongside the FBI and DEA. So let me say the part my fellow privacy skeptics often leave out: a license plate reader is a genuinely useful tool.  When a suspect fled the Brown University shooting […]
text:
The nearly 300 Flock Safety cameras installed across Rhode Island remain mostly unregulated. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)I spent 20 years as a police officer, commanded the Investigative Services Division, and worked a federal drug task force alongside the FBI and DEA. So let me say the part my fellow privacy skeptics often leave out: a license plate reader is a genuinely useful tool. 
When a suspect fled the Brown University shooting last December, plate-reader technology helped find him fast. These cameras recover stolen cars, flag vehicles tied to open cases, and feed the AMBER and Silver alerts that bring missing children and vulnerable seniors home. I have run investigations that would have closed faster with that kind of lead, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
That is exactly why I want you to pay attention to what Rhode Island is doing with them. The tool is not the problem. The absence of rules is.
There are now nearly 300 Flock Safety cameras operating in Rhode Island, most installed through a federal grant that put 39 of them across more than 20 communities at no local cost. And they are, as the ACLU accurately puts it, virtually unregulated. We have no state law governing how long the data is kept, who may search it, or which outside agencies get to reach into it. The company now deletes records after seven days by default after a recent policy change — it previously held onto data for 30 days. The Rhode Island State Police say every search requires a case number, an offense, and a reason. I believe them. I also know, from the inside, that an internal policy is only a promise, and a promise is not oversight.



Quotation







The tool is not the problem. The absence of rules is.


Look at what happens elsewhere when the promise is all there is. In Dayton, Ohio, an audit found more than 7,000 searches of the city’s own cameras run for immigration purposes expressly banned by city policy. In Illinois, federal Customs and Border Protection reached state plate data through a pilot program the company later said its own leadership did not know about. In Milwaukee, an officer used the system more than a hundred times to track a woman he was involved with. None of that is hypothetical, and all of it happened inside systems that also had guardrails and stated reasons.
Here is the uncomfortable truth for anyone who has worn the badge: Self-policing is not accountability. I trusted the officers I worked with, and most earned it. But a network that logs the movements of every driver in the state, innocent or not, and can share them with agencies in other states or in Washington, is not something you secure with good intentions. You secure it with law.
My own town of Warren looked at this squarely and said no, one of only two councils in the state to reject the state police request outright. Its members did not claim the cameras are useless. They worried that once the data exists, control over it can quietly expand, and residents had no guarantee their movements would not be shared without consent. South Kingstown reached the same conclusion and canceled its contract. Others are now revisiting theirs. These are not paranoid towns. They are asking the question the state skipped.
I do not want Rhode Island to throw the tool away. I want it to grow up about how it uses it, with a real law rather than a vendor’s terms of service. Mandatory public hearings before any camera goes up. A public, searchable log of who queried the system and why. Enforceable limits on retention. And an absolute prohibition on sharing our data for federal immigration enforcement or for tracking anyone who crossed a state line for lawful medical care. If a search cannot survive daylight, it should not happen.
Some will say that ties the hands of good cops. I was one, for two decades. Good policing is not weakened by transparency. It is strengthened by it, because the moment one officer misuses this network the way officers already have elsewhere, every legitimate case built on it becomes suspect. Trust leaves an institution one shortcut at a time, and it does not come back easily.
The cameras are not watching for criminals. They watch everyone, and sort it out later. That may be a bargain worth making. But we should make it on purpose, in the open, with rules we wrote and can enforce, not inherit it by grant application while no one was paying attention.

name: VTDigger
title: Plan would double St. Johnsbury homeless shelter beds, free up space for families
description:
About 10 to 15 people are typically waiting for a bed to open up at the existing Moose River Drive shelter. The new building, about a quarter mile away, would help meet that need.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Plan would double St. Johnsbury homeless shelter beds, free up space for families.
text:
The former Moose Lodge in St. Johnsbury, photographed in June 2026. April McCullum/Vermont Public
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
More emergency shelter capacity is in the works in St. Johnsbury.
The Northeast Kingdom nonprofit developer Rural Edge is under contract for a former Moose Lodge, which it plans to convert into a 40-bed, low-barrier shelter. The anti-poverty organization Northeast Kingdom Community Action is set to operate the site.
The two groups joined forces three years ago to open the region’s only year-round, general-occupancy homeless shelter, quickly converting an old church into 20 emergency beds after a new state law cleared zoning restrictions for the site. 
Once the Moose Lodge location is ready for occupancy, the organizations plan to transition individuals from the existing shelter on Moose River Drive to the new space. Then, they’ll convert the old building into a shelter specifically for families. There are currently no dedicated family shelters in the Northeast Kingdom. 
“The need for emergency shelter has never been greater in the Northeast Kingdom,” said Jenna O’Farrell, executive director of Northeast Kingdom Community Action, in a press release. “Expanding The Shelter at Moose River will allow us to serve more of our neighbors during times of crisis while strengthening the support systems that help people transition to stable, permanent housing.”
After state cutbacks to the pandemic-era motel voucher program, the community has seen increased need for shelter options, said Patrick Shattuck, executive director of Rural Edge. According to Northeast Kingdom Community Action, the Moose River Drive shelter currently gets about 10 referrals a week, and maintains a waitlist of 10 to 15 people.

The existing shelter on Moose River Drive in St. Johnsbury, seen on Oct. 19, 2023. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public and VTDigger

The groups originally looked at building out more space at the Moose River Drive location, but decided it would be too challenging to keep all guests sheltered while the renovations were underway, Shattuck said. Then the Moose Lodge, a large, single-story building about a quarter mile away, came up for sale.
Rural Edge hopes to finalize the acquisition of the Moose Lodge building by the end of this year, with the aim of opening the new shelter before the 2027-2028 winter season. The renovated space will contain semi-private individual spaces for guests.
As of May 2026, there were over 100 households experiencing homelessness in Caledonia and Essex counties, according to Coordinated Entry data. A regional housing study from 2023 found that over 2,100 households in the Northeast Kingdom were on waiting lists for subsidized rental housing – more than 3.5 households for every unit.
The purchase of the new building costs about $460,000, Shattuck said. Preliminary estimates to renovate both the existing shelter and the new space total about $4 million, he said. Earlier this summer, Rural Edge received $50,000 from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board to advance plans for the project, and is currently soliciting donations.
St. Johnsbury Town Manager Chad Whitehead said he’s only received positive feedback from neighbors about the current shelter location. He sees the need for expanded options, as he’s observed people sleeping outside of the downtown Welcome Center.
“There are people that recently have been sleeping on the porch. That’s not a long-term solution for anybody, especially as winter gets here,” he said.
