name: Maryland Matters
title: Worcester County schools blend culture, tenure, individual attention to earn top test scores
description: Worcester County Schools Superintendent Annette has a mantra: Name. Strength. Need. Know every student’s name, their strength and their need. It's just one of the factors that have helped make the Eastern Shore system tops on state assessments for several years.
text:
Pocomoke Elementary third-grade teacher Jennifer Copenhaver looks over the student job assignments Aug. 25 in preparation for the first day of school in Worcester County. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Jennifer Copenhaver was getting her colorful third-grade classroom at Worcester County’s Pocomoke Elementary School ready last week — big-screen Smart TV, an oversized blue bean bag and one pink flamingo propped on a light blue bookshelf, waiting for about 20 students Monday.
“I can’t wait,” Copenhaver, a 15-year teaching veteran who’s entering her second year at Pocomoke Elementary, said Tuesday. “It’s feels like a community here [in Worcester] because everybody’s so inclusive and loving and caring. Everybody really, really cares about the kids and wants to do what’s best for the students.”
That shows up in test scores for Pocomoke Elementary, a Title 1 school that receives additional resources due to the number of economically disadvantaged students there. It achieved a four-star rating out of five on a state report card.
But Pocomoke is just one example of the “wonderful things going on” in the Worcester County school district, which has achieved the highest level of proficiency on the Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program in math two years and in English for the last three years.
Nearly 70% of Worcester students were deemed proficient in English testing this spring, compared to 68.5% last year and 69.4% in 2024. The state proficiency rate this year was 52%.
Worcester students also had the state’s highest level of math proficiency at about 49% this spring — the state rate was 27% — and 47.7% last year. The district ranked second in the state two years ago, with a math proficiency rate of 39.3% of students.
About 7,130 students will be greeted by 650 teachers when doors open Monday morning.
Five of the county’s six elementaries were four-star schools in 2024-25 school year — the sixth was not eligible that year — as were all three middle schools. One of its three high schools got four stars while the other two received five stars on the state’s annual report card.
A sign near the Worcester County public schools administration building. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Sharon Donahue-Conway has had two children graduate from Worcester’s Stephen Decatur High School and go on to college, and her youngest child, age 12, will begin the sixth grade at Berlin Intermediate School. She said she’s been “very happy with Worcester County Public Schools and the teachers,” but added that parents must help teachers and administrators.
“At home, we reinforce the importance of education. The teacher is not there to just say you’re doing great when you suck,” she said in an interview Wednesday. “It’s like no one’s going to applaud you and give you a ribbon for doing the minimal. I think you just have to reinforce that not everything is easy and not everything is online. Real life happens offline.”
Donahue-Conway said one countywide initiative she’s pleased with is how the school system stresses the importance of test scores with student achievement.
“We were always prepared to know when the testing was going to happen, and that was great,” she said.
In-house assessments
 The preparation for students to take standardized tests starts with schools conducting “in-house assessments,” which former Superintendent Lou Taylor stressed “is not teaching to the test.”
The assessments, Taylor said, allow staff to evaluate each student’s strength and weakness. It not only boosts student achievement, but also boosts students’ confidence in future test-taking. The reading assessments used are Kindergarten Reading Assessment, or KRA, DIBELS and i-Ready.
“Then teams of teachers take a look at every individual kid, where they’re weak and where they’re strong, and then aggressively working with those individuals to build those weak areas,” Taylor said. “So that when the Maryland assessments take place, we have spent some time in those areas. These are just proficiency skills that kids need at grade level.”
Taylor retired in June 2025, after nine years as superintendent. He worked in education for 41 years, all in Worcester County. He said the in-house assessments initiative began during former superintendent Jon Andes’ tenure between 1996 to 2012. Andes currently serves on the county’s school board.
Taylor, who won in this year’s Republican primary election for the District 6 seat on the Worcester County Board of Commissioners, said small class sizes are another reason for the school district’s academic success.
Pocomoke Elementary kindergarten teacher Katie Sipple said she will begin the school year with 15 students. While that could increase during the school year, she said, colleagues in neighboring school districts like Wicomico County have more than 20 students from the start.
“I’m able to meet with more kids than if I was to have 25 to 30 kiddos,” Sipple said in a classroom illuminated by some lamps and bright stars strung along the ceiling. “I’m able to pull kiddos, whether it’s one-on-one or in a small group. Just having that small class size, I’m able to sit at more tables and see more kids and talk to more kids.”
Worcester County Superintendent Annette Wallace, left, chats with kindergarten teacher Katie Sipple on Aug. 25 insider her Pocomoke Elementary School classroom. Wallace’s niece will be a student in Sipple’s class. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
One of the new children that will enter Sipple’s classroom is the niece of Worcester County Superintendent Annette Wallace.
“Keep up the good work, but be ready for her. She’s something else, in a good way,” Wallace said to Stipple as they both chuckled.
‘We’re all educators’
Like Wallace, some of the teachers and administrators have longevity in the school district. Wallace graduated from Snow Hill High School in 1999, earned a bachelor’s degree in math from Salisbury University in 2003 and was hired by Taylor as a math teacher at Stephen Decatur High School.
After working as an assistant principal and principal at Pocomoke High School (and being named Maryland principal of the year in 2016), and then as chief operating officer and academics officer, Wallace succeeded Taylor to become the district’s first female superintendent on July 1, 2025.
Under her leadership, Wallace demands not only support staff, teachers and administrators help students succeed, but every single person that works in a school.
“I believe public education is a ministry,” she said. “I told our staff that … when I met with everybody. Whatever your religion is, or whatever you believe in, this is not a job. When you come here, you’re going to work harder than you’ve ever worked, but you’re also going to get to experience joy and a sense of being a part of something bigger like you’ve never had before. We’re all educators.”
One mantra Wallace continues to push: Name. Strength. Need.
Know every student’s name. Know every student’s strength. Know every student’s need.
“Why? Well, because everyone wants you to know their name, because when you know my name and you can say my name and you can identify me, then I know I belong here, by my strength,” she said. “I don’t want to be known by my needs. I want you to know my needs, but when you say to me, Annette Wallace, I want you to say all the wonderful characteristics about me. So, when we think about our kids, it’s the same story.”
When Wallace visits a school, the plan is to deliver some books to students. She continues to be irked that 109 third graders were not proficient in reading this past school year.
“That’s not OK,” she said.
Wallace’s passion was mentioned during last month’s state Board of Education by State Superintendent Carey Wright. During a brief interview Friday morning, Wright called Wallace “relentless,” especially when it comes to monitoring data.
“Annette is a very unique person. She could tell you down to the name of every third-grade student that wasn’t reading at grade level,” Wright said. “She makes sure all those kids get the intervention that they need. I think that’s one thing about her, is that she’s constantly looking for other ways to provide access and opportunity for her students to continue to grow and thrive.”
‘Some respect’
Working in Worcester County was the only place that made sense for some of the staff such as Pocomoke Elementary Principal Melissa Freistat, entering her 26th year in education in the county.
Pocomoke Elementary School first-grade teacher Mckenzie Munson talks about preparing her classroom last week for Monday’s first day of school in Worcester County. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
First-grade teacher Mckenzie Munson, also head coach of the Pocomoke High School’s field hockey team, is only going on her fourth year teaching at the school. She graduated in 2018 from Pocomoke High School down the street, and stayed on the Shore to earn a bachelor’s degree in elementary education from Salisbury University in 2022.
“She’s a baby,” Freistat said jokingly.
Even with the generational difference, Freistat and Munson both love Worcester schools. However, they said the district could be even better with some help from the state.
For instance, invest in dedicated spaces for early childhood education within or separate from a school building. A Judy Center that serves children from infant to age 5 moved back from Pocomoke High School to Pocomoke Elementary.
Besides encouraging visits to the district, Wallace had one simple solution for state legislators: “Put some respect on our name, is what I would say. Start asking people working in schools how things should be done.”
Copenhaver, the third-grade teacher who’s also trained in social-emotional learning, said the state should mandate that training for all teachers. She recalled times during her teaching career, at schools other than Pocomoke Elementary, when she’s had to deal with physical altercations between students.
Copenhaver said it’s important to teach not only academics, but also the right way to treat people.
“One thing I tell my students: You don’t have to like everyone, but you have to be respectful,” she said. “I know they can do the work … but if they can’t handle themselves in the appropriate way, there’s no way they’re going to learn everything they need to learn to be productive human beings in society.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Nearly two years into prison term, Jamey Noel still owes nearly $2 million in restitution
description: Nearly two years after former Clark County Sheriff Jamey Noel was sentenced to prison for stealing millions in public funds, he and two family members still owe nearly $2.7 million in court-ordered restitution. Washington County court records show more than $1.26 million from three accounts holding proceeds from the Noel family’s liquidated assets was distri[...]
text:
Jamey Noel reads a prepared statement on Monday, Oct. 14, 2024, at a Clark County Circuit Court hearing in Jeffersonville, Indiana. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Nearly two years after former Clark County Sheriff Jamey Noel was sentenced to prison for stealing millions in public funds, he and two family members still owe nearly $2.7 million in court-ordered restitution.
Washington County court records show more than $1.26 million from three accounts holding proceeds from the Noel family’s liquidated assets was distributed in January. Nearly $978,000 went to the nonprofit organization that operated New Chapel EMS, while roughly $286,000 went toward restitution owed to state and local government agencies.
But most of the debt remains.
Jamey Noel, his estranged wife, Misty, and their daughter Kasey collectively still owe more than $2.66 million to the Utica Township Volunteer Fire Fighters Association, which did business as New Chapel EMS and provided ambulance service in Clark and Floyd counties.
Jamey Noel also owes another $17,774 to the state on behalf of the Clark County Sheriff’s Department, according to court accounting records obtained by the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Nearly $2 million of the remaining debt is Jamey Noel’s alone. Misty Noel owes the association $586,424, while Kasey Noel owes another $90,600.
Washington County Clerk Stephanie Rockey said the escrow and accounting records will be updated as the court orders additional transactions.
More than $1.2 million distributed
The distributions were completed Jan. 30 under a settlement combining criminal restitution and overlapping civil claims involving Jamey, Misty and Kasey Noel.
Rockey’s office issued a $286,413 check to the Indiana Attorney General’s Office. A court order allocated that money toward debts owed to the Indiana State Police, Indiana Department of Revenue and Clark County Sheriff’s Department, including tax restitution owed by all three Noels.
Matt Owen, chief executive officer of the firefighters’ association, received three checks totaling $977,836.
Story continues below.
Order Granting (2)
 
The largest payment — $885,393 — came from proceeds collected in Jamey Noel’s case. Another $74,382 came from Misty Noel’s account, and $18,061 came from Kasey Noel’s case.
Those payments reduced — but did not eliminate — the Noels’ largest restitution obligations.
Jamey Noel was ordered to repay the association $2.87 million as part of his 2024 plea agreement. Misty Noel was ordered to pay it $660,807, and Kasey Noel was assessed another $108,661.
The Washington County accounts now hold a combined $30,015: about $29,762 in Misty Noel’s account, $253 in Jamey Noel’s account and nothing in Kasey Noel’s.
A separate Clark County court order distributed roughly $900,000 from civil-case escrow accounts in January. Those funds included payments to the Attorney General’s Office, the Utica Township Fire Protection District and the firefighters’ association.
More property sold
Asset sales have continued even after the larger settlement.
A judge authorized four additional vehicles and a utility trailer titled to Jamey Noel to be sold through Clayton-based Freije & Freije Auctioneers this year. The four vehicles brought a combined $5,850 at the company’s May Big Boy Toy Auction in Indianapolis.
A 1962 Cadillac Fleetwood and a 1975 Cadillac ambulance each sold for $2,000, a 1954 Plymouth Belvedere fetched $1,600, and a 1968 Chrysler Imperial brought just $250, according to Freije & Freije.
The utility trailer was sold later for $4,200, bringing the five assets’ combined hammer price to $10,050.
As assets sell off, former Sheriff Jamey Noel inches toward multimillion-dollar restitution orders

None of those proceeds has yet been remitted to the Clark County court, however. Freije & Freije said it was waiting for the court to provide one final vehicle title before deducting auction expenses and sending the net proceeds to the clerk.
An amended order entered Aug. 24 corrected the identity of the Cadillac ambulance sold at the auction and authorized a new title. The order said the mistake occurred during an inventory of approximately 56 vehicles seized in the Noel investigation.
Still, the relatively modest proceeds are a fraction of the money generated by earlier sales.
As of November 2025, auctions and forced property sales had generated more than $2.7 million, although mortgages, liens, commissions and other expenses reduced the amount available for restitution. A May 2025 auction of 43 classic vehicles alone generated nearly $1.28 million.
Other sales included firearms, Rolex watches, custom suits, furniture, tools and multiple homes owned by Noel and his family.
Noel pleaded guilty in 2024 to 27 felony charges, including corrupt business influence, theft, tax evasion and official misconduct. Investigators found that he used money belonging to New Chapel EMS and other public entities to finance vehicles, travel, clothing, college expenses and other personal spending.
He received a 15-year sentence, with three years suspended to probation. The continuing restitution effort has unfolded across multiple criminal and civil cases while Noel serves the prison portion of that sentence.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana takes a step toward adopting Medicaid work requirements
description: Louisiana’s proposed work requirements for Medicaid enrollment largely adhere to the new guidelines Congress and President Donald Trump laid out last year. The new state regulations are expected to go into effect for Medicaid recipients in January.
text:
Louisiana's new work requirements for Medicaid are expected to go into effect in January. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Louisiana’s proposed work requirements for Medicaid enrollment largely adhere to the new guidelines Congress and President Donald Trump laid out last year. The new state regulations are expected to go into effect for Medicaid recipients in January.
The proposed rules would necessitate many Medicaid enrollees between 19 and 65 years old to earn at least $580 per month or complete at least 80 hours per month at a job or volunteer opportunity in order to qualify for benefits. They may also enroll in school or job training part-time to meet the requirement. 

The state health department first published the proposed work requirements in July and gathered public comments about the plan during August. They must clear a few more legal steps before being permanently adopted into law. 
Medicaid provides health insurance coverage for lower-income, pregnant and disabled people. Critics of the incoming work requirements said the restrictions will end up pulling benefits from many who should qualify for the assistance. 

“Most people who lose coverage [due to work requirements] end up losing it for paperwork reasons … not because they aren’t working or refuse to work,” said Jan Moller, executive director of Invest in Louisiana, a public policy group that advocates for low-income families. 
Louisiana anticipates at least some people will be cut from the Medicaid program as a result of the work requirements. A state financial analysis published alongside the proposed rules in July estimates healthcare providers in the state will lose out on $14 million in the current fiscal year and $88 million in the fiscal year that starts July 1, 2027, from work requirements taking effect. 
State analyses accompanying the publication of the proposed work requirements also concluded they would have a “negative impact” on “family functioning, stability and autonomy,” as well as the state poverty rate.
The proposed rules provide for several exceptions to the work obligations for Medicaid recipients, however. 
Adults who aged out of the foster care system will continue to get their health coverage through Medicaid until they are age 26, regardless of whether they meet the work requirements. Likewise, people who receive Medicaid coverage because they are pregnant or postpartum won’t need to meet work obligations. 

People in treatment programs for substance abuse will also be exempt. Those who have been incarcerated will also qualify for Medicaid without fullfilling the work requirements for the first 90 days after their release.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

Medicaid recipients who are the parent or guardian of someone under age 14 or a person with a disability also won’t be required to meet the work obligations. 
Critics worry at least one of these exemptions is likely to be confusing for Medicaid participants. 

Following federal guidance, Louisiana’s proposed state rules would allow people to avoid the work requirements if they are deemed “medically frail.” 
Until a few months ago, many health care experts assumed “medically frail” would correlate to certain serious medical diagnoses outlined in a law Congress passed in 2025. But the latest set of federal rules indicates recipients will have to take extra steps starting in 2028 to prove their condition qualifies as one that makes it too difficult for them to work, volunteer or attend school. 
It’s not clear what documentation the “medically frail” enrollees will have to provide to keep their coverage. Democrat-led states are suing to stop this particular restriction from taking effect.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Maryland Matters
title: The plight of the Blueprint: a deeper dive
description: The Blueprint for Maryland's Future is admirable for the ambitious goals it set for the state's schools, but some achieving those goals is proving to be a challenge for local school systems, writes Kalman Hettleman, who says it's time for a course correction.
text:
The 10-year Blueprint for Maryland's Future education reforms are ambitious, but it's proving to be a challenge for local school systems to meet those goals. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)It’s back to school and high hopes. Teachers will work tirelessly — but they won’t get the help they deserve from the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future
I wrote in July about the discouraging test scores of Maryland schoolchildren and deteriorating hopes for the success of the Blueprint. I have been criticized by some (applauded by others) for my gloomy warning signals.
Let me further explain.
At first, there were widespread loud cheers for the Blueprint’s development. And deservedly so. The ambition of the Blueprint far surpasses any other state’s school reform efforts.
And significant progress has occurred on preschool enrollments, reduced teacher vacancies, growth in dual enrollments in college courses, more teachers earning National Board Certification, and the huge increase in community schools.
Nonetheless, over the past five years or so, sharp criticism has accelerated. For the most part, the disillusionment has focused on the Blueprint’s unrealistic expectations — too much to do and too little time and money to pull it off.
Still, Gov. Wes Moore and the General Assembly keep kicking the Blueprint can down the road.
The Blueprint Accountability and Implementation Board also has substantial sway to put in motion a plan for course correction. But it’s come up short.
This failure is evident in the recent update of its Comprehensive Implementation Plan (CIP). The CIP is supposed to hold the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) and 24 local school districts (LEAs) accountable for effective implementation of the Blueprint. Yet. the CIP neglects the Blueprint’s most fundamental flaws: manageability and credibility.
Manageability




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Manageability (sorry for the clunky term) is more essential to Blueprint implementation at this point than more funding.
Unfortunately, the Kirwan Commission (on which I served) and the General Assembly in enacting the Blueprint did not pay close enough attention to the fact that MSDE and the 24 LEAs could not possibly effectively implement such a massive and unprecedented array of tasks.
Consider the length, breadth and depth of Blueprint expectations. Approximate page counts are staggering: the Blueprint law (236); the CIP (192); and “Implementation Considerations” in the CIP (233). Further, the CIP includes over 600 tasks and sub-tasks that MSDE and LEAs must do.
The Public School Superintendents’ Association has counted 179 reports that local districts must provide under the Blueprint and other related state or federal legislation.
The Blueprint Coalition, of about 40 organizations and individuals (me included), has repeatedly pointed out a persistent and widening gap between stated goals, required actions, and the status of implementation.
In other words, the Kirwan Commission and the General Assembly bit off more than state and local educators could chew — despite whole-hearted efforts all around.
Credibility
The Comprehensive Implementation Plan is not a true plan. It lacks basic and vital accountability measures.
For example, the CIP  calls for AIB “to … create a timeline for implementing the Blueprint.” Such timelines don’t generally exist.
What’s more, the CIP largely ignores the gaps between CIP goals and actual implementation so far. To illustrate, the CIP sets an expectation that “All third-graders are reading on grade level by FY 2027.” However, given the current data in which only about 30% of third graders are reading on grade level, the chances are nil that all third-graders will be reading on grade level by 2027 — or even when the Blueprint sunsets in the early 2030s.
The Blueprint Coalition has noted that the CIP lacks a credible assessment of whether implementation is actually occurring as promised.
Recommendations

The governor and General Assembly must require realistic, manageable goals aligned with available resources.
The AIB should revise the CIP to set timelines and address areas where implementation is significantly lagging.
The AIB should begin to provide annual reports, overdue under the Blueprint, that assess Blueprint progress, including whether funding is adequate.

In fairness, the AIB, like MSDE and LEAs, has been given unrealistic duties that are beyond its own resources and authority. It has performed admirably, but it lacks the powers of the governor and General Assembly. Still, it could do more.
And the governor and General Assembly could do much more.
Course correction is overdue.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Data shows NH Child Care Scholarship Program is being used more than ever before
description: With the price of childcare for New Hampshire families rivaling college tuition, more are looking to the state’s scholarship program for assistance. New data shows that in the past fiscal year, usage of the program increased, while the state is spending over $12 million more than the previous year.  The New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship […]
text:
A New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program sticker adorns a door at Rochester Child Care Center. In the most recent state fiscal year, more families used the scholarship than ever before. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)With the price of childcare for New Hampshire families rivaling college tuition, more are looking to the state’s scholarship program for assistance. New data shows that in the past fiscal year, usage of the program increased, while the state is spending over $12 million more than the previous year. 
The New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program is a subsidy voucher program that helps eligible families pay for childcare and out-of-school time care for children under age 13, or 18 if they have a disability. The state directly pays childcare programs a predetermined weekly standard rate, and parents pay a copayment towards tuition depending on their level of eligibility. 
The 2026 fiscal year, which ended June 30, brought the largest increase in usage of the scholarship that the state has seen. On average, 4,979 children were using the state scholarship in the past year, up from an average of 3,984. 


Since 2024, scholarship usage has increased by 75%, after declining during the COVID-19 pandemic. The number of children enrolled in the program also increased after the eligibility requirements for the program expanded to include more families. 
In order to be eligible for the program, parents must have children in the eligible age range, meet the activity requirement —have a job, be looking for a job, or be in school or a training program— and have a household income that is eligible. 
In 2023, the state Legislature expanded the rate of eligibility for the scholarship program to 85% of the state median income, meaning that families whose household income was less than that became eligible for the first time. Changes went into effect in 2024. 
With increased usage came increased costs. Since 2024, expenditure for the scholarship has more than doubled, and the state has diversified how it pays for it. 


The childcare scholarship program is funded using federal Child Care and Development subsidies and some state general dollars. Federal law allows some Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, funding to be used as well, under a strict set of rules. 
According to Dow Drukker, senior policy analyst at the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, around 76% of scholarship dollars were funded using TANF dollars in the second quarter of 2026. Over the past 12 months, about 33% of scholarship expenditures have come from TANF, a larger percentage of TANF usage compared to past years. 
“That’s not unusual to over rely on federal dollars, given towards the end of fiscal year, agencies want to use up their federal dollars,” he said. 
Under the guidance of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, the state Department of Health and Human Services maximized the amount of TANF money eligible for childcare use to prevent a waitlist for the scholarship. 

 
 
Monthly costs for the scholarship program vary for a number of reasons, according to officials at the Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration. Holidays, summer vacation, and the new school year, when many children age out, all impact the number of children enrolled, connected to a provider, and receiving care. 
Every few months, the bureau presents scholarship information to the Child Care Advisory Committee, including the number of children enrolled in the scholarship program but not connected to providers and actively receiving care. The majority of children who fit this categorization are school-age children. The department does not track individual cases of why children would not be connected. 


While enrollment in the scholarship is up, only a small number of eligible children in the state are using it. According to a 2024 UNH Carsey School of Public Policy study, over 55,000 children under age 13 are eligible for the scholarship. The study cites lack of awareness, substantial paperwork, and complexities in maintaining eligibility as possible reasons. 
Also, of the state’s early childhood and school-age programs, only about 70% to 80% of childcare programs statewide accept scholarship funds. 
Some providers have said the state’s reimbursement system does not account for the “true cost” of providing childcare and would prefer to not offer it to avoid dealing with the paperwork. 
Scholarship reimbursement rates to providers are redetermined every three years when the state submits its plan to the federal government on how it will use the Child Care and Development Fund. The plan requires each state to submit its findings from a recent market rate survey, which asks questions of providers to determine the “price tag” of childcare tuition and help set reimbursement and cost share rates. The next survey will start in October and will be run by the Carsey School and the bureau. 
According to data from the Fiscal Policy Institute, the average cost of childcare for a two-parent household with a 4-year-old and infant in New Hampshire was about $30,000, costing families about 24% of a family’s income. The federal government recommends 7% of a family’s income go toward childcare. 
As scholarship enrollment increases, Drukker said there could be a potential “fiscal bottleneck” concern in the future regarding funding for the scholarship program. The program’s increased usage, along with New Hampshire only contributing the minimum dollar requirement to the program, could lead to some “big questions.” 
“We’re leaning pretty heavily on (TANF),” Drukker said. “What do the next six months look like, and what does that mean for the scholarship program? Because we haven’t had a waitlist since 2011.”

title: A summer of recalls exposes holes in the nation’s food safety net
description: Jalapenos. Frozen berries. Beef. Alfalfa sprouts. A summer of food recalls, including the record-shattering cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce that has sickened thousands, has raised many Americans’ fears of contracting a foodborne illness. The recalls have focused attention on the Trump administration’s decision to cut funding and staff at seve[...]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. A summer of food recalls, including the record-shattering cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce that has sickened thousands, has raised many Americans’ fears of contracting a foodborne illness. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Jalapenos. Frozen berries. Beef. Alfalfa sprouts.
A summer of food recalls, including the record-shattering cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce that has sickened thousands, has raised many Americans’ fears of contracting a foodborne illness.
The recalls have focused attention on the Trump administration’s decision to cut funding and staff at several public health agencies, and prompted questions about whether those changes have made consumers more vulnerable.
In fact, this year’s tally of food recalls is roughly in line with the numbers in recent years. About 48 million people each year get sick from a foodborne illness. But experts worry that the scope, severity and scale of outbreaks and their associated food recalls are growing.
While the United States sees some cyclosporiasis cases every year, this year’s outbreak has crushed records: Since May, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed more than 17,000 cases, with another nearly 12,000 reported cases still under investigation. The outbreak has resulted in at least 922 hospitalizations and two deaths.
Federal officials have blamed this year’s multistate outbreak on processed iceberg lettuce from central Mexico. The lettuce was brought to the U.S. by Taylor Farms, a distributor that supplies foods to thousands of restaurants and grocery stores, including Target, Taco Bell, Whole Foods, Kroger, Walmart, Costco and Jack in the Box.



Quotation







I think there are valid questions around the timing of the response, the time it took for agencies to recognize the outbreak and to start to investigate it, get boots on the ground in Mexico.


– Jennifer McEntire, food microbiologist and founder of Food Safety Strategy


The CDC and the Food and Drug Administration are investigating at least six other clusters for which a source hasn’t yet been confirmed.
Cuts at the CDC and FDA haven’t necessarily increased consumers’ chances of food contamination or outbreaks, said Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and the founder of a food safety consulting firm. However, McIntire said, “I do think the cuts may have influenced the way outbreaks unfold.”
“I think there are valid questions around the timing of the response, the time it took for agencies to recognize the outbreak and to start to investigate it, get boots on the ground in Mexico,” she said.
Darin Detwiler, a food safety expert and professor emeritus at Northeastern University, noted that the U.S. is seeing more recalls affecting multiple states, rather than a small area. He added that more recalls are being tied to a problem earlier in the food chain — such as contaminated irrigation water at a large lettuce farm rather than, say, improperly stored deli meat at a sandwich shop  — which can spread the pathogen to a far higher number of people and make it harder to track and contain.
“We’re seeing so many people impacted, so many states impacted, and the recalls are dragging on for a long time,” Detwiler. “There’s ambiguity or lack of transparency over who’s even behind a recall.”
The White House dismissed concerns about the federal government’s ability to handle outbreaks.
“The Trump Administration has never cut FDA food inspectors or other frontline personnel for domestic disease response,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Stateline in an email. “President Trump’s top priority is the health and safety of the American people, and the federal government remains capable of robustly addressing any future outbreaks.”
Fewer staff, less funding
Last year, the Trump administration laid off thousands of employees at federal public health agencies including the CDC, which tracks and responds to disease outbreaks, and the FDA, which oversees and regulates food safety.
While some of the layoffs were reversed through lawsuits or by Congress, the nation’s health public agencies remain at diminished capacity. The CDC workforce has been reduced by 28% since December 2024, the month before Trump took office, according to a Stateline analysis of data from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management. Employee numbers at the FDA are down 23% during the same period.
Last year, U.S. inspections of foreign food facilities, such as the Mexican farming operation linked to the cyclospora outbreak, plummeted to historic lows following those staffing cuts. The FDA suspended a quality control program for food testing. And the parasite surveillance staff at the CDC, which responds to outbreaks, was downsized last year by the Department of Government Efficiency from 11 people to three.
Sandra Eskin, a food safety expert who worked in the office of food safety at the U.S. Department of Agriculture during the Biden administration, likened federal public health cuts to the game Jenga, where players construct a tower of wooden blocks and then remove the blocks one at a time while trying not to make the tower fall.
“I think that’s what we’re seeing,” said Eskin, who now leads a public health nonprofit called Stop Foodborne Illness, which advocates for stronger food safety policies. “Whether it’s cuts in staff, cuts in funding that trickle down to the states, or late responses to outbreaks — these are all pieces of wood in that game where you start pulling them out and then the whole thing collapses.”
The federal government also has delayed requiring companies to comply with new food safety rules, included in a law enacted more than a decade ago, that would help regulators track where food comes from and where it’s going during outbreaks.
Detwiler and other experts say the new rules could have helped speed the government’s sluggish response to the cyclospora outbreak investigation after Taylor Farms initially tried delaying the recall.
Last year, the Trump administration also drastically scaled back FoodNet, an early warning surveillance system that required tracking of infections caused by eight different foodborne pathogens. The federal-state collaboration is now only required to track two pathogens: salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E.coli. The other six pathogens, including cyclospora, were made optional.
The CDC says the change was made because other surveillance systems monitor those pathogens. But McEntire and other food safety experts want them reinstated on FoodNet.
State impacts
Infectious outbreaks like cyclosporiasis are typically investigated by state and local health departments, which largely rely on federal dollars distributed through the FDA and CDC. Public health has been chronically underfunded for decades under several administrations, experts say.
But the Trump administration since last year has terminated $5.78 billion in CDC grants — funds that were appropriated by Congress but had not yet been spent.
Michigan, at the center of the cyclosporiasis outbreak with the highest number of cases and clusters, is one of 23 states (plus the District of Columbia) that successfully sued the Trump administration in June 2025 over federal funding cuts.
Changes to federal funding last year affected public health infrastructure across Michigan, a representative from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services told Stateline. During the cyclosporiasis  outbreak, the state used its own resources to bolster local responses.
“While we are able to support this investigation on a local level, sustained investment in public health capacity is essential to ensuring Michigan can respond effectively to future regional and statewide public health threats,” said department spokesperson Lynn Sutfin.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana said no to phones in school. Now parents have to say it at home.
description: As the new school year starts Indiana students will spend their school day without the constant pull of smartphones. Gov. Mike Braun and the Indiana General Assembly deserve credit for recognizing what teachers have known for years: children cannot learn when every lesson competes with a notification. In an era when nearly every issue becomes […]
text:
Students in Indiana school this year have a new bell-to-bell cellphone ban. (Getty Images)As the new school year starts Indiana students will spend their school day without the constant pull of smartphones. Gov. Mike Braun and the Indiana General Assembly deserve credit for recognizing what teachers have known for years: children cannot learn when every lesson competes with a notification. In an era when nearly every issue becomes political, this one should not.
Indiana’s new bell-to-bell cellphone law is one of the most meaningful child wellness policies our state has adopted in recent years. The average American teenager spends more than seven hours a day on screens outside of school, more time than most of them sleep, and among heavy users, roughly one in four reports symptoms of anxiety or depression. Teen depression doubled between 2011 and 2021, a period that tracks almost exactly with the rise of smartphones as constant companions. The law sends a clear message that schools exist to educate children, not to compete with social media companies for their attention.  
As a physician, I applaud that decision. As a father, I know it is not enough. I remember a night not long ago when my daughter was telling me about her day while I nodded along, phone in hand, half-reading an email I had already read twice. She stopped talking. Not because she was angry. Not because she was hurt. She simply learned, somewhere along the way, that she was competing with something she could not beat. That moment has stayed with me far longer than the email ever did.
If a physician who spends his career studying health behavior still struggles with these habits, I can only imagine how difficult they are to overcome after a long shift or a day that left nothing in reserve. We are raising children in a world deliberately designed to distract all of us. For years, we have asked schools to solve a problem we created at home.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The biggest obstacle to this law’s success is not sitting in a classroom. It is sitting around our dinner tables. It is resting in our pockets. Our children are watching us far more than they are listening to us. We tell them to put their phones away in class, then they watch us answer texts during dinner. We tell them to pay attention, then they watch us interrupt conversations because our watch vibrated. We tell them relationships matter, then they watch us choose a screen over the people sitting beside us. Children learn far more from what we model than from what we say.
Parents sometimes talk about smartphones as though they simply appeared in childhood. They did not. Children do not buy smartphones. They do not pay wireless bills. They do not decide whether phones belong at the dinner table, in bedrooms, or on family vacations. Those decisions belong to us and that reality is uncomfortable precisely because it places responsibility exactly where it belongs.
These platforms are not designed to help our children put them down. They are designed to keep them scrolling. Every notification is engineered to capture one thing: attention. Adults struggle to resist that same pull, and we should not be surprised that children do too. Schools can set boundaries during the day, but only parents can shape habits for life.
That does not require an elaborate family technology plan. It begins with a few quiet decisions. Phones stay off the dinner table. They charge in the kitchen instead of the bedroom. When your child wants to tell you about their day, your phone stays in your pocket. Not because they need another lecture about screen time, but because they need your undivided attention, and they will remember whether you gave it to them.
Perhaps the defining parenting mistake of the past decade has been confusing presence with availability. We have made ourselves available to everyone through our phones while becoming less present for the people sitting right in front of us. Those are not the same thing, and children understand the difference even if they cannot explain it. We cannot ask schools to teach attention while we model distraction.
The state has acted. In signing this law, Braun did something rare in American politics: he prioritized the long-term health of children over short-term convenience. Now it is time for parents to do the same.  Years from now, our children probably will not remember whether we answered one more email or responded to one more text. They will remember whether we looked up.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Restoring energy sanity: New Hampshire must break free from utility-driven costs
description: New Hampshire residents and businesses are feeling the pressure of what can only be described as an energy squeeze. Rising electricity and fuel costs are hitting household budgets and cutting into already thin business margins. For many, energy has become one of the most unpredictable and burdensome expenses they face. These rising costs aren’t happening […]
text:
"New Hampshire needs to move beyond the idea that energy policy must be an either-or debate." (Photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire residents and businesses are feeling the pressure of what can only be described as an energy squeeze. Rising electricity and fuel costs are hitting household budgets and cutting into already thin business margins. For many, energy has become one of the most unpredictable and burdensome expenses they face.
These rising costs aren’t happening in a vacuum either. Global instability continues to affect fuel supply and pricing, while New England’s rigid energy structure limits how effectively we can respond to that volatility. As a result, we end up with a system that leaves ratepayers exposed to this volatility with little ability to adapt. If we truly want to ease this pressure, we need to rethink how our energy is procured and managed. That starts with moving away from a passive, utility-dependent model toward a more flexible, locally driven approach.
The failure of traditional utility models
Traditional utility procurement models are a main component of the overall problem. Most utilities purchase energy in short, six-month segments, and while this may simplify regulatory oversight, it limits the ability to take advantage of favorable market conditions. When prices spike, there ends up being little to no protection for consumers. This structure also reinforces dependence on external energy sources and global markets that are beyond our control.
At the same time, the region’s energy mix presents even more challenges. Renewable energy, particularly solar, plays an important role in reducing emissions and diversifying supply. However, in parts of New England, solar development has outpaced investments in storage and grid infrastructure, and without sufficient storage to capture and distribute that energy when it is needed most, costs associated with delivery and system balancing can rise. Ratepayers ultimately absorb those costs.
The municipal solution: Lessons from CCA programs
Believe it or not, there is a better way forward, and some New Hampshire communities are already leading the way. Community Choice Aggregation, or CCA for short, allows municipalities to take a more active role in purchasing energy on behalf of their residents and businesses. As opposed to relying solely on utility procurement, communities can pursue strategies that reflect local priorities and market opportunities. Several municipalities, including Laconia, Londonderry, Merrimack, Salem, and Windham, have already embraced this approach, with their experiences demonstrating how local control can translate into real savings and greater stability.
Salem offers a clear example. By taking a strategic approach to timing and contract structure, the town was able to shield its residents from some of the worst effects of recent market volatility. Instead of locking into short-term agreements, Salem pursued a longer-term, flexible strategy that allowed it to respond to these changing conditions. As of right now, Salem has projected savings of more than $825,000 in just the first few months of the program.
This kind of outcome isn’t a one-off situation. Instead of treating energy procurement as a routine administrative function, it becomes an active, market-aware process.
The third path: An all-of-the-above strategy
Looking more broadly, New Hampshire needs to move beyond the idea that energy policy must be an either-or debate. Too often, discussions are framed as a choice between traditional fuels and renewables, or between cost and sustainability, when in reality, the most effective path forward is one that blends multiple approaches.
An all-of-the-above strategy, or “third path,” recognizes that reliability, affordability, and environmental responsibility must work together. Renewable energy should continue to expand, but it must be supported by investments in storage and grid modernization. At the same time, access to reliable domestic energy sources, including natural gas, remains essential to maintaining stability, particularly during peak demand and in winter months.
Policy tools such as net metering need to evolve as well. While it has played an important role in encouraging renewable adoption, future policies should better reflect the needs of the grid as a whole, as a more balanced approach can ensure that incentives align with system reliability and long-term cost control.
A call for energy independence
Ultimately, the choices we make about energy are economic choices. These decisions affect competitiveness, household stability, and the overall health of our communities. Continuing with the status quo means accepting ongoing volatility and rising costs driven by factors outside our control.
What New Hampshire needs to know is that they have another option. By empowering municipalities, embracing flexible procurement strategies, and pursuing a balanced energy portfolio, the state can build a more resilient system, one that protects residents and businesses from future price shocks while supporting long-term sustainability.
The energy squeeze is real, but it is not inevitable. With the right approach, New Hampshire can take back control and restore a measure of sanity to its energy future.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Milquetoast Marshall flees from Kansans and hides from reporters. Somehow, he still wants your vote!
description: Put down your coffee. Set the bran muffin aside. I have an exclusive for Kansas Reflector readers this morning. Here’s the complete list of public, in-person campaign events planned by U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas. … … … … … … Looks great, right? Marshall claims to be on a 120-stop tour of Kansas, […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall speaks at a Kansas Chamber event on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)Put down your coffee. Set the bran muffin aside. I have an exclusive for Kansas Reflector readers this morning. Here’s the complete list of public, in-person campaign events planned by U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas.
…
… …
… … …
Looks great, right?
Marshall claims to be on a 120-stop tour of Kansas, but his adventures across the Sunflower State have been conducted almost entirely in private, behind closed doors and without advance warning of his stops.
They’re not listed on his campaign website. Trust me, I looked.
They’re not listed on his campaign Facebook page, either. The events section stops in 2020.
With a few exceptions, members of the news media have not been invited to observe, and members of the public have been blocked from attending or asking the senator questions. His campaign hasn’t informed Kansas Reflector about those tour plans, preferring to post pretty pictures on social media.
Marshall offered an excuse in comments to the Hays Post.
“The town halls just became non-productive and dangerous, not just dangerous for myself, but dangerous for my staff and dangerous for the people in the audience as well, so I just don’t think that they’re safe to do,” Marshall said.
You might notice that Marshall used the word “dangerous” three times in that quote, perhaps attempting to persuade himself that public events carried some sort of actual risk.
They don’t, and Marshall knows it. He and his staff have never been physically unsafe, but they have faced outraged constituents.
He can’t stand the heat, so he’s beating a hasty retreat from the kitchen.
You could watch temperatures rise during the senator’s March 1, 2025, event in Oakley Kansas, where constituents turned out in force. They demanded answers about the brutal idiocy of President Donald Trump‘s administration, embodied by the ill-named Department of Government Efficiency.
Clearly rattled, Marshall fled the scene 20 minutes early. He later fantasized that paid agitators were behind the event.
His chief of staff, Brent Robertson, smeared the audience: “Real Kansans overwhelmingly support President Trump’s DOGE initiative, shrinking the size of the federal government, and firing career bureaucrats. Local Oakley citizens had no clue who these people were and were embarrassed by the behavior.”
“Real Kansans” only support Roger Marshall? Puh-leeze. Incidentally, Politico reported in October 2025 that Robertson had charged taxpayers $44,000 for commuting between Washington, D.C., and his home in Lynchburg, Virginia.
A Virginian should know about “real Kansans,” I guess!
In the 17 months since the Oakley debacle, Marshall has not held a single open, public, in-person event. Access to the senator has been tightly controlled. Even scheduling a debate between him and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton has turned into a partisan sniping match. Marshall apparently hopes to get away without answering any questions at all.
He probably hoped to get away with the same approach to his reelection campaign. Democrats haven’t won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas since 1932 and can usually be counted on to faceplant. In the meantime, Marshall’s office guided a “coordinated effort” to fill his spot with a Republican if he had to resign for, you know, reasons.
That’s all to say I don’t think our favorite Florida man expected that he would have to spend time and effort in this dry Midwestern state. We don’t even have oceanfront property!
Please note that these criticisms have nothing whatsoever to do with Marshall’s party or beliefs or governing philosophy.
He’s been an odious rubber stamp for Trump and provided cover for an appalling evisceration of public health. But those are different columns for different times. As a candidate for public office, Marshall needs to make a public case. He has appeared frequently enough on D.C. talk shows to prove he can handle himself.
Apparently, though, he’s only comfortable taking tough questions from people in tailored suits and designer outfits. And only after he spends some time in a professional makeup artist’s chair.
You have to campaign.
That means meeting people who aren’t on a pre-approved list. That means answering questions that didn’t go through a pre-screening process. That means, yes, interacting with dastardly journalists now and then. The people of Kansas are not a danger to Marshall. They do not wish him ill. They simply want him to face them honestly, in person, and answer questions.
The only danger out there for Marshall, and it seems like a real enough one in these early days of the fall campaign, is that he actually loses his seat.
Perhaps that’s why he’s running scared. 
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” comes out Sept. 29 from the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Maine Morning Star
title: Limits of ‘affordability checks’ surface as payments begin to arrive in mailboxes
description: Kathleen Anderson, 75, doesn’t have to file taxes because her income comes from monthly Social Security checks. But this year, Anderson had to file in order to be eligible for a $300 payment from the state.  Anderson, who lives in an affordable senior housing community in Fairfield, said she’s lucky to have a case manager […]
text:
Fairfield resident Kathleen Anderson has been helping people in her affordable senior housing community file their taxes so that they are able to receive the $300 affordability checks being mailed to Mainers with lower incomes. (Photo courtesy of Kathleen Anderson)Kathleen Anderson, 75, doesn’t have to file taxes because her income comes from monthly Social Security checks. But this year, Anderson had to file in order to be eligible for a $300 payment from the state. 
Anderson, who lives in an affordable senior housing community in Fairfield, said she’s lucky to have a case manager for her disability who informed her of the opportunity and taught her how to file her taxes, which is not the case for many of her neighbors. 
“There are lots of people who don’t have computers in my building,” Anderson said. “And, there are people who certainly can’t deal with the [tax] form. It’s too complicated.” 
Despite being eligible for the “affordability checks,” which were a cornerstone of the latest state budget, Mainers who are solely reliant on Social Security or disability will not receive them unless they file taxes, which they otherwise aren’t required to do. 
The checks are automatically mailed to Maine residents of certain incomes who file a 2025 Maine individual income tax return. Approximately 514,000 Mainers are eligible, and the state has processed just over 237,000 checks as of last week, according to Sharon Huntley, director of communications for the Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services.
It’s likely that about two-thirds of Social Security recipients in Maine are eligible, but given the lack of data on people who don’t file taxes, it’s a difficult figure to pinpoint. 
Several of the Mainers who have received or are waiting to receive checks told Maine Morning Star that the $300 will make at least some difference in their ability to pay for essentials such as utility bills. But many also pointed to the ways the one-time payments fall short of addressing persistent affordability issues. 
“It’s been kind of a very sad game of ‘which need and whose need’ should I try to address with this $300, and I haven’t come up with a good answer,” said Hazel Willow, a mother who now relies on government assistance after an abusive relationship left her in financial strain. 
The state is starting to mail $300 checks to some Mainers. Are you eligible?

Barriers 
Anderson has been helping people in her building file their taxes, in some cases loaning out her  computer to do so, especially since free help is otherwise sparse given that the American Association of Retired Persons’ preparation services close at the end of tax season. Anderson has also heard from several people who are skeptical that the checks are real. 
When her neighbor, Suzanne Varney, 63, first heard about the initiative, she thought it was a scam. 
“I’m not going to hold my breath until I actually see a check in my mailbox,” Varney said. 
But the check landed in her mailbox about a week ago, after Anderson helped her file her taxes, which she does not usually have to do because she relies on disability. 
“If it wasn’t for her, I would lose out because I don’t know how to do my taxes,” Varney said of Anderson. “I get stressed out and then I get overwhelmed and then I want to shut down.”
Given these barriers, Varney said it would be useful for case managers, home workers or other trusted support workers who help people with low incomes to inform their clients about the checks. 
Full-year Maine residents who file their 2025 state return by October 15 are eligible if they have a federal adjusted gross income of less than $100,000 if filing a joint return, $75,000 if filing as a head of household, or $50,000 if single or married filing separately. People who are able to be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s 2025 individual income tax return are not eligible. 
Anderson questions why eligibility was tied to tax returns and not based on reliance on certain government services. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Maine gave bonus payments to workers collecting unemployment insurance. 
But there are limits to such an approach, in part because state law restricts access to health and human services data. There are also many low income people who don’t apply for assistance programs even though they are eligible, said James Myall, policy analyst for the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Huntley said the $300 affordability payments were created to return a portion of Maine sales and excise tax payments to individuals considered to be disproportionately affected by such taxes. 
Gov. Janet Mills proposed the checks in her final budget before terming out at the end of this year, which the Democratic majority in the Legislature agreed to include but at a lesser amount, ultimately settling on a $155.2 million price tag. Republicans criticized the move but so did some Democrats, particularly given the checks’ limited and short-term impact.
As the checks have begun to get mailed out, Myall has also heard some complaints about people just missing the threshold of eligibility, which lawmakers had lowered to reduce the cost, though he noted that the $300 is likely to go farther with people who have the least. 
Limits 
“For me personally, that’s a lot of money,” Varney said. 
Varney plans to put most of it toward bills, including car expenses she had to put on a credit card and has been trying to pay off.  
For Anderson, who said she gets roughly $1,240 a month from Social Security and currently has $8 in her checking account, $300 will help pay her bills and fill her car with gas. Anderson said she also plans to put some of it toward essentials like toilet paper and dish soap, which are not covered by food stamps.  
Willow similarly plans to focus on paying down debts, such as her power bill. “I’ve already had my power shut off twice in the past year and it is so psychologically destabilizing and physiologically destabilizing,” she said. 
But she’s balancing the need to do that against paying for medications for post-traumatic stress disorder and other health issues that are not covered by insurance, or getting back-to-school clothes for her child. 
Five years out of an abusive relationship and into living in poverty, Willow said, “I’m doing everything I can to get off of these supports because it feels awful, and I just, I wouldn’t wish this on my worst enemy.” 
While the $300 will make a difference, she said she wants to see more state investment in programs that offer recurring payments or services such as childcare that would have a long-term impact on quality of life and mental health. 
“I know how to stretch $1,” Willow said, “but it just feels a little bit like it’ll kind of evaporate by the time it gets here. It’s not that I’m not grateful, but it’s kind of like a Band-Aid on a bullet hole.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: ACA premium prices insuring 900K Georgians to shoot up – again
description: The Affordable Care Act health insurance program that covers 900,000 Georgians is on track to see price hikes of as much as 20% or more when open enrollment begins this fall for 2027 coverage. That’s according to state data obtained by the Georgia Recorder for the ACA exchange run by the state and called Georgia […]
text:
The across-the-board increases for Affordable Care Act plans in Georgia come on the heels of a round of increases caused by the expiration of pandemic-era enhanced subsides. Ariel Hart/Georgia RecorderThe Affordable Care Act health insurance program that covers 900,000 Georgians is on track to see price hikes of as much as 20% or more when open enrollment begins this fall for 2027 coverage. That’s according to state data obtained by the Georgia Recorder for the ACA exchange run by the state and called Georgia Access.
Next year’s inflation is on top of massive price increases that already occurred for 2026 coverage after Congress and President Donald Trump allowed pandemic-era extra ACA subsidies to expire. 
The insurance companies’ proposed price increases on the Georgia marketplace are not final. First, the numbers might still change because they are from the mid-summer negotiation point, said Bryce Rawson, a spokesman for the Georgia Office of the Commissioner of Insurance. Prices are finalized before open enrollment begins Nov. 1. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In addition, the premium price changes that consumers see when they go to sign up at open enrollment will also be affected by how federal and state subsidies are calculated.


Inflation: Health Insurance Edition
The Affordable Care Act marketplace in Georgia, called Georgia Access, is expecting price increases for 2027 health insurance coverage. The data below is as of late August 2026. Final prices will translate to individual premiums for purchase on GeorgiaAccess.gov on Nov. 1, 2026.
Insurer Proposed increase from 2026 to 2027:
Alliant 29%
Ambetter 10%
AMGP 25%
Antidote New to the market in 2027
BCBS/Anthem 21%
CareSource 21%
Cigna Leaving the market in 2027
Kaiser 20%
Oscar 28%
UnitedHealthcare Leaving the market in 2027
Source: Georgia Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire


But the news is a signal and a blow to customers, as well as to the hospitals who wonder if this means more are going to walk in uninsured next year in need of free care. A lobbyist for hospitals in Georgia, Monty Veazey, said that the massive price increase that already took effect this year threw so many people off the ACA exchange that Georgia hospitals lost $441 million, based on his calculations of the average value per insured person. 
Carry Smith, an ACA customer in coastal Georgia, was terse when told about the coming price increases. Smith juggles multiple part-time jobs and has depended on her ACA plan to keep a life-threatening infection at bay. 
Smith’s premium insurance skyrocketed seven-fold earlier this year, and she managed because she had just paid off her car. She couldn’t say exactly how she plans to pay her premium if it increases yet again. Hearing the possible numbers, Smith said, simply, “Wow.”
Nora Pullen, a resident of Fayette County. Pullen is one of many self-employed Georgia businesspeople who dropped their ACA health insurance policies in 2026 after federal subsidies expired. She wants them restored. (Photo courtesy of Nora Pullen)
Nora Pullen, a self-employed life and wellness coach and math and testing tutor in Fayette County, already dropped her ACA coverage this year after prices skyrocketed. She had little hope that prices would come back within reach this year but this seals it. 
“I honestly don’t think this is sustainable for people,” Pullen said, when told about the planned increases.
Pullen is a Democratic activist but the decisions are being felt across the political spectrum. 
However, the decisions to drop coverage are weighted in one camp: those who are healthy, like Pullen. Those who are in immediate need of care, like Smith, are more likely to stay. And that becomes a corporate Catch-22 where it’s even more expensive for insurance companies to keep providing coverage, causing them to raise prices yet again.
“It is not a good indication of where the market’s going, to see two years of extremely steep increases like this,” said Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the Program on the ACA at the health research nonprofit KFF. “What we’re seeing is that insurers are saying that they’re kind of expecting the market to continue shrinking. In other words, more people becoming uninsured, likely because it would be the healthier people who leave the market, and that’s what’s making premiums go up.”
After the last round of price increases, Georgia saw about 350,000 people drop their ACA insurance from spring of 2025 to spring of 2026, one of the largest drops in the nation. That’s partly because Georgia didn’t expand Medicaid to all its poor, so huge numbers of Georgians just above the poverty level are instead insured through Georgia Access.
Georgia Access enrollment now stands at about 900,000, according to the state.
Some advocates, like Veazey, also blame insurance companies for taking advantage of the moment to make even more profits. The one insurer in Georgia that has a lower price increase this year is Ambetter, part of Centene Corporation. They already did a price increase of 38% for Georgia ACA plans last time, so this year they’re only raising prices here by 10%. That’s still far ahead of most other inflation, but the company has touted such moves as part of its financial comeback this year, according to Forbes, leading to a $1 billion profit just in the last quarter. Centene did not respond to those criticisms Friday afternoon.
What all this means in the end is that more people will drop insurance, said Veazey, president of the Georgia Alliance of Community Hospitals. That means that more people will hold off on going to the doctor when they should, and they won’t seek care till they’re worse. And then when they do, it won’t be to the doctor; they’ll walk into his members’ emergency rooms, because that’s the one place where federal law mandates that people be stabilized no matter their ability to pay.
“It’s not good for us, nor is it good for the patient,” Veazey said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: ‘Springfield is under siege right now.’ ICE agents in Ohio have detained two Haitian pastors
description: More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status earlier this summer.  Faith leaders recently spoke out against the ICE activity that has been taking place in the Clark County city after a June decision by the U.S. Supreme Court […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield, Ohio, after temporary protected status for Haitians ended on July 27, 2026. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status earlier this summer. 
Faith leaders recently spoke out against the ICE activity that has been taking place in the Clark County city after a June decision by the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country. Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27.
Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil is a TPS holder with an asylum case pending. 
“I am calling out this administration to tell them that we deserve to be treated with dignity,” he said. “We deserve to be treated as human beings. We are not animals.”
Dorsainvil is one of about 15,000 Haitians who live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.
“They are not a threat to the community,” Dorsainvil said. 
First Baptist Church Pastor Adam Banks said Haitian people are not “political bargaining chips.”
Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil (left) and Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church (right) speaking to the media in Springfield, Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“They are not threats to be monitored and removed,” he said. “They are care providers, co-workers, faith leaders, and family. … We demand an end to deportations that tear families and our community apart.”
ICE agents are detaining people in Springfield in shopping plazas, gas stations, and apartment complexes. 
“Springfield is under siege right now,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.
Fellow Springfield pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien was detained by ICE agents on Aug. 20 and advocates are calling for his release.
“We hope that will happen very, very soon,” Ruby said. “He needs to be out immediately. He is a good man with a congregation to serve, and they are without a pastor right now.”
A pastor from the First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield was detained last week when he was in Northwest Ohio and he might be out of the country already, according to Ruby.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Many Haitians detained in Springfield by ICE are being sent to Butler County Jail in Hamilton, which had 1,103 total inmates as of Friday afternoon.
The general housing capacity for Butler County Jail is 844, even though the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction recommends 756 as the housing capacity, according to a 2025 ODRC inspection report.  
Haitians living in Springfield are being required to report to ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville and wear ankle monitors. 
“Being outfitted with that monitor, it just symbolizes slavery,” Dorsainvil said. 
He shared the story of a mother who came to the Haitian Support Center, having given birth a few weeks prior, but lost the baby.
“She could not even walk, but they put the shackle on her,” Dorsainvil said. “You cannot understand how hard it is to hear those people on a daily basis crying.”



Quotation







They are afraid to go out. They do not have freedom to go out. They don't have the freedom even to look for help.


– Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of Springfield's Haitian Support Center


Advocates are calling for an end to the ankle monitors. 
“It is inhumane,” Ruby said. “It is an insult. It is designed to humiliate, and we want it to stop right now.”
The pastor recently helped a Haitian family relocate to Canada. 
“Their children had survived kidnapping attempts when they were in Haiti,” he said. “Most families can’t go to Canada. It was only an option for this family because they had an immediate family member who was there.”
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency. 
A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June. 
The federal government promised Haitians who self-deport a free airplane ticket and a $2,600 check to return to Haiti. 
“They are not getting the money that our government has promised,” Ruby said.
He talked to a reporter in Haiti who shared that Haitians who are being deported are getting off the plane and running for their lives. 
 “It puts a target on them that says to the gangs, ‘come get this person.’ ” 
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X or on Bluesky.
