When: Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. Doors open at 7 p.m.; concert begins at 8 p.m.
Where: The Queen, 500 N. Market St., Wilmington
Admission: Tickets start at $50
Benefiting: Donate Delaware
Honoring: State Rep. Debra Heffernan
Tickets: Ticketmaster
Sponsorships and host committee information: Contact Brian McGlinchey at brian@queenjeansball.com
Learn more: Donate Delaware or The Queen

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri kratom company destroys $10M in products after DEA crackdown
description: Kansas City-based CBD American Shaman says it destroyed $10 million worth of product this week after the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration placed a potent kratom-related opioid manufactured by the company into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act. The DEA on Wednesday temporarily scheduled mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, along with two related compounds[...]
text:
Todd Blanche, who was confirmed as attorney general on Aug. 8, appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill (Eric Lee/Getty Images).Kansas City-based CBD American Shaman says it destroyed $10 million worth of product this week after the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration placed a potent kratom-related opioid manufactured by the company into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act.
The DEA on Wednesday temporarily scheduled mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, along with two related compounds known as MGM-15 and MGM-16. Schedule I is the federal government’s most restrictive category for controlled substances and includes heroin.
“These are potent opioids being manufactured and sold in consumer products, often under labels that obscure their true risks,” U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release. “This action will protect our nation’s children and communities from the dangers of drug addiction and abuse.”
The order will remain in effect for two years. It was issued months after the agency announced its plans to temporarily schedule these three compounds, along with another related substance, 7-hydroxymitragynine above specified concentration thresholds. The feds have not yet issued an order on 7-OH.
Vince Sanders, owner of Kansas-City-based CBD American Shaman, said his company produces the majority of mitragynine-pseudoindoxyl products nationwide. Earlier this week, after learning the federal order was coming, his team destroyed about $10 million worth of product “at cost, not at retail value,” he said.
“Unfortunately, of all the things, pseudoindoxyl is probably the very best pain medicine ever to hit Earth,” Sanders said. “I mean, very little mind change, very slow addictive properties, and just an incredible painkiller. But it’s gone. I’m sure it’ll show up as a pharmaceutical in five years or so, but as of now, people don’t have it available, which is truly a shame.”
Sanders said his company didn’t manufacture MGM products because it was “less studied and more potent.” However, his best-selling products contain 7-OH, and Sanders’ company has led the nation in manufacturing them.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway sued American Shaman in March, taking particular aim at 7-OH products that she called “hazardous opioids.” The company agreed to immediately suspend all in-state sales of 7-OH. 
The DEA made clear the action is directed at “deliberately manufactured and concentrated opioid products, not traditional botanical kratom.”
Kratom leaves, or Mitragyna speciosa, come from a tropical tree found in Southeast Asia. They can be crushed and then smoked, brewed with tea or placed into gel capsules.
The leaves contain an alkaloid called mitragynine. During digestion, the body converts it into 7-OH in small amounts. It’s what gives people the opioid-like effect.
The products the DEA is targeting contain a highly concentrated amount of 7-OH by taking mitragynine and chemically oxidizing it. The DEA described the three compounds rescheduled Wednesday as “chemical rearrangements” or “derivatives” of 7-OH.
“These products are commonly sold in different forms such as powders, tablets, and liquid shots,” the DEA’s order states. “This is a significant evolution from the traditional administration of Mitragyna speciosa, which was once restricted to either chewing raw leaves or steeping the leaves into water decoctions and teas.”
Products with mitragynine pseudoindoxyl first appeared on the market in 2024, the order states, and MGM-15 a year later. 
According to the order, a study on products sold online containing mitragynine pseudoindoxyl showed that of the 51 total available products, 35 had an appealing flavor, such as berry, lemonade and watermelon. And 32 of the products had packaging with bright colors. Seventy-six percent of these products were chewable tablets, with the rest being liquids or candy-like products.
Among the products sampled, 71% featured a combination of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and 7-OH, while 24% contained mitragynine pseudoindoxyl only. 
The DEA’s proposed order for 7-OH products would generally cover processed or synthetic products containing more than 0.05% 7-OH or more than 1 milligram of the compound per article, along with botanical kratom containing more than 0.05% 7-OH by dry weight.
Christopher McCurdy, a professor at the University of Florida’s College of Pharmacy, said he understands the DEA’s concern but he doesn’t agree with placing the compounds in Schedule 1. 
“I agree with the standpoint that these shouldn’t be accessible by anybody at a gas station, smoke shop where you can easily buy some of these materials without any kind of medical supervision,” McCurdy said. “But it’s just going to more than likely create a more gray market where these products are being sold without the ingredients being disclosed.”
McCurdy points to a recent study he co-authored on the mislabeling of kratom-derived products. He’s also concerned about what it will mean for research teams like his who are studying these compounds. From a research standpoint, he said it’s very difficult to work with a Schedule 1 substance.
Sanders argues the temporary rescheduling came down to politics. 
“At the end of the day, who loses is the American consumer who desperately needs these products,” he said. “It’s just really sad. It just shows that when you have greed coupled with political power, what can happen.”
He pointed to a new congressional inquiry into the kratom industry’s ties to the Trump administration.
The U.S. Senate Committee on Finance’s ranking Democratic member, U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon., has called for an investigation into a possible conflict of interest related to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin’s advocacy for restrictions on 7-OH. Wyden is requiring information to be provided to the committee by the end of the month, related to Mullin holding a financial stake in Oklahoma-based Botanic Tonics — a competitor of 7-OH products — reportedly worth as much as $1 million.
The order states that published scientific literature has not established mitragynine pseudoindoxyl as a naturally occurring kratom alkaloid. However, scientific and analytical questions remain about whether it may be reported at incidental trace levels in some botanical products as a result of processing, storage or analytical conditions.
“In light of these unresolved questions, the Department of Justice will exercise enforcement discretion when only incidental trace amounts of MGPI are confirmed in a product otherwise consistent with botanical kratom,” the department’s news release states. “This policy does not create a legal exemption and does not change MGPI’s status as a schedule I controlled substance.”
While the department explains this enforcement discretion in the news release, it’s not stated in the temporary order itself, said Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association.
On Thursday, the American Kratom Association filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking declaratory and injunctive relief to confirm this point.‍
“The AKA supports aggressive enforcement against chemically manipulated MGPI, MGM-15, and MGM-16 products,” Maddow said. “But responsible kratom consumers and legitimate botanical kratom businesses should not be put at risk because trace-level chemistry is detected in otherwise traditional botanical kratom.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Service will memorialize site of Emmett Till’s slaying
description: Emmett Till was beaten, tortured and killed in this barn on Aug. 28, 1955.
text:
On Saturday, the barn where Emmett Till was tortured and killed will take its first step toward becoming a public memorial.
“For the first time since his lynching, this site is no longer someone’s shed, where they kept their personal belongings, but it will be used as a reverent memorial for Till’s life and legacy,” said Patrick Weems, executive director of the Emmett Till Interpretive Center.
Since the 2024 publishing of Wright Thompson’s best-selling book, “The Barn,” about the site, center attendance has nearly doubled from 2,000 or 3,000 a year to about 5,000 people. Another 25,000 a year are seeing the center’s traveling exhibits on Till.
Although the barn is not open to the public, several hundred people have visited it informally since the center purchased the barn in November, resulting in far more traffic than before, Weems said.
“People go out of their way to find us. We don’t advertise. It’s word of mouth.”
A mob of white men killed Till, a Black teenager visiting from Chicago, on Aug. 28, 1955. His mother, Mamie, insisted on opening his casket “so that the world could see what they did to my boy.” That act helped spark the modern Civil Rights Movement.
Saturday’s memorial service will honor the mother and son. Visitors will gather at 9 a.m. at the Mound Bayou Museum of African-American Culture & History and ride in a caravan to the barn for a wreath laying and concert by the Mississippi Mass Choir, followed by the service.
Emmett Till and his mother, Mamie Till-Mobley.
“Preserving this barn where Emmett Till was murdered is as important as preserving the balcony of the Lorraine Motel where Martin Luther King stood when he was shot,” said Devery Anderson, who is updating his book, “Emmett Till: The Murder That Shocked the World and Propelled the Civil Rights Movement,” to include the memorial.
Now that the barn is in the center’s hands, he said, people can go beyond reading about this history — they can touch it.
The first time he stood there, Anderson said he thought about “the beating, screams and bloodshed that happened in that very spot, the killers crouching over Till as he took his final breath.”
Tears flowed from Anderson’s eyes. “I knew I was on sacred ground.”
In recent decades, the barn in the Mississippi Delta belonged to a local dentist. Television producer Shonda Rhimes donated $1.5 million needed to buy the property and the barn — a purchase that drew some criticism.
“Of all the Emmett Till sites, this was the hardest to decide whether to purchase it or not,” Weems said. “We landed on yes. If we’re going to tell the truth about what happened to him, you have to have the barn. It’s ground zero.”
Patrick Weems, co-founder of the Emmett Till Interpretive Center, takes a look at the new Emmett Till river marker during a rededication ceremony for the marker on River Road in Glendora Thursday, June 21, 2018. Credit: Eric J. Shelton, Mississippi Today/ Report for America
Since its purchase in November, officials have built a privacy wall to separate the barn from the previous owner’s property. They are now working on transforming it into a place of memory, Weems said.
“We not only want to honor Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley, but the witnesses who testified against the killers,” he said. “Willie Reed knew full well the consequences he would suffer for telling the truth, and he did it anyway.”
On the day Till was killed, Reed was walking down the road when he saw a truck drive past and head to the barn. There were four white men and three Black men as well as someone hunkered down in the truck.
At the 1955 murder trial of Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, Reed testified that he heard screams and “licks like somebody was whipping somebody,” coming from the barn. He also identified Milam as the one who emerged from the barn to get a drink.
After torturing Till, who had just turned 14, the killers shot him dead and dumped his body into the Tallahatchie River, where he was found three days later.
In spite of Reed’s testimony, the all-white jury acquitted the killers, who justified their torture and murder of Till because he reportedly whistled at Bryant’s wife.
Reed fled to Chicago, changed his name and died in 2013 without fanfare.
The center has purchased adjacent property near where Reed’s home was located and plans to honor him there as well as turning the barn into a memorial space, Weems said.
The dream is to create parking spaces on the adjacent property and have visitors cross on a bridge over the cypress bayou to the barn, he said. Plans also include the restoration of the barn to the way it looked in 1955, he said. “We’re hoping to raise the resources to do that.”
Darryl Johnson Jr. is the former mayor of Mound Bayou and pastor of the Walk of Faith Covenant Church.  Credit: Courtesy of Emmett Till Interpretive Center
Overall plans are still in progress, he said. “How do you honor Emmett Till? How do you honor Willie Reed?”
Darryl Johnson Jr., former mayor of Mound Bayou and pastor of the Walk of Faith Covenant Church, said after starting the Mound Bayou museum, he saw the importance of Mamie Till-Mobley’s courage. She wouldn’t let the injustice done to her son die with him, he said.
“People who support the justification given to kill that young man are still hiding the truth,” he said. “We have to face the truth so that we can receive the love of God, and the way we participate in his love is by loving our fellow man.”
Ashley Nelson, a writer who formerly worked for the International Coalition of Sites of Conscience, visited the site for the first time in July.
“I don’t think anyone stands untouched at Auschwitz,” she said. “The same is true at the barn.”
Gloria Dickerson, who leads the Emmett Till Academy in Drew, grew up hearing her mother talk about the barn where Till was killed, but she didn’t visit it until six or seven years ago. The barn brought back memories of her mother and reminders of what “African Americans have gone through in Mississippi,” she said. “It was emotional.”
Gloria Dickerson of Drew is the founder of We2together Creating Change. She grew up close to the barn where Emmett Till was tortured and killed. Credit: Courtesy of We2together
Making the barn a memorial preserves history and provides a place for reflection and healing. “We’re going to heal ourselves and move forward,” she said. “The fight is not over.”
Vonkerius Jackson, program facilitator for Carrying Our Voices, took several Indianola High School students to visit the barn. “You forget that he was barely 14, and the barn is so dark and lonely,” he said. “To hear the history of it was just, ‘Wow.’”
The hate that led to Till’s slaying, though, has never vanished, he said. “It’s crazy how quiet racism can be and how bold it can be at other times.”
He pointed to the sign memorializing Till, which was shot hundreds of times and had to be replaced with one that was bullet-proof, he said.
After visiting the barn and the center, Jackson learned how much Till loved to joke and laugh. “Nobody talks about how he brought so much joy to the world,” he said.
The visit made Till come alive, he said. “It humanizes his history and inspires me. We have to keep his history alive. The truth is, Mississippi’s history never dies; it just keeps on going in a circle.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas City groups band together in wake of surprise storm’s severe damage, slow government response
description: KANSAS CITY, Kan. — In the absence of immediate government response, community organizations in Kansas City, Kansas, banded together to help each other reckon with the effects of a tornado-like storm that damaged homes, trees and power lines without much warning. It wasn’t until days later that government agencies arrived to help to the predominantly […]
text:
Nikki Richardson-Iwegbu on Aug. 19, 2026 speaks with Kansas City, Kansas, community members in the wake of a destructive storm that likely caused millions in damage to homes, infrastructure and possessions. (Photo by Matt Kleinmann)KANSAS CITY, Kan. — In the absence of immediate government response, community organizations in Kansas City, Kansas, banded together to help each other reckon with the effects of a tornado-like storm that damaged homes, trees and power lines without much warning.
It wasn’t until days later that government agencies arrived to help to the predominantly Black community.
When storms began rolling through northeast Kansas the night of Aug. 18, Nikki Richardson-Iwegbu said “it felt as though I did something wrong and somebody was attacking me.”
Violent hail woke her up at 1:36 a.m. Aug. 19, and she moved into her bathroom for shelter, waiting for a tornado siren.
“I just waited,” she said, “and then you hear destruction. Power goes out, and I’m just sitting there waiting, just waiting, just to see what’s going to happen.”
A siren never sounded.
“Then the storm goes away, and I instinctively know, OK, in the morning you’re going to get in your car, and you’re going to see, what was that?” she said.
Nikki Richardson-Iwegbu, co-founder of Justice for Wyandotte, on Aug. 19, 2026, roams the streets of northeast Kansas City, Kansas, in the immediate aftermath of a major storm that damaged the area, pulling together volunteers, resources and an emergency response structure along with other community members. (Photo by Matt Kleinmann)
A storm cell brought downburst winds, horizontal hail and tornado-like gusts of 70-80 mph, inflicting millions of dollars in damage and knocking out power for nearly 25,000 homes, but meteorologists have refrained from calling it a tornado.
“The big difference is that tornadoes are going to result in a different type of damage path,” said Alex Krull, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Kansas City, Missouri. 
Tornadoes cause damage by shifting inward and then upward, but this storm involved strong east-west and downward winds. 
Krull said the storm that hit Kansas City, Kansas, was most akin to the type of damage an EF0 tornado might cause, which involves wind gusts from 65-85 mph.
The first severe thunderstorm warning was issued in northeast Kansas at 12:38 a.m. Aug. 19, Krull said. The second warning, which overlapped eastern parts of Wyandotte County, including where some of the most extensive damage occurred, was issued at 1 a.m. and was set to expire at 1:45 a.m.
The third and final warning issued before the last storm cell containing the downburst was issued at 1:40 a.m. The heaviest damage occurred between 1:40 and 1:50 a.m., Krull said.
Roswell Church of Christ is one of two churches in Kansas City, Kansas, damaged by a tornado-like storm that ravaged the area in the early morning ours of Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Matt Kleinmann)
On Thursday, kids scaled a pile of chainsawed tree limbs like it was playground equipment while utility trucks and tree removal service trucks made their rounds in northeast and northwest Kansas City, Kansas. 
Roswell Church of Christ had covered the gaping hole left in its roof, and residential streets were lined with piles of debris. On Wednesday, 10 volunteer electricians crisscrossed the area providing free repairs. 
Richardson-Iwegbu, executive director of the nonprofit Justice for Wyandotte, created a plan of action with two other community organizers — Matt Kleinmann and Randy George, co-founder of the Village Initiative — the morning after the storm to respond to the emergency needs left in the wake.
It made sense to them that a social justice organization born out of police accountability work was the one to mobilize volunteers to respond to a natural disaster. Justice for Wyandotte has built trust in Kansas City, Kansas, where the government has lost it.
“Instinctively, our organization is not designed to immediately rely on local government,” Richardson-Iwegbu said.
Its mission is to help communities sustain themselves so they don’t need to rely on the government for help, she said, because many people in northeast Kansas City, Kansas, feel harmed by local government systems, including law enforcement agencies.
“It’s hard for you to ask them to rely on a system that they feel has failed them, so we oftentimes try to be that conduit,” she said.
For the first five days after the storm, the group was in survival mode, Richardson-Iwegbu said.
She said she didn’t recall seeing emergency responders that morning.
“I’ve never been in a storm response before, so I don’t know what was supposed to happen,” she said, “but I just knew that I still was not seeing the government presence that I expected to see that matched the destruction that I knew just happened. There still felt like a disconnect.”
Kleinmann, a former Democratic candidate for state and federal office, doesn’t attribute the disconnect to negligence. Some people didn’t know they needed to have home insurance to protect against a destructive storm, and the government, he said, didn’t appear to know initially how to respond.
Even though the storm disconnected the neighborhood’s power, Kleinmann said, it connected community members “more than it had in a really long time.”
In an interview Thursday, Richardson-Iwegbu said the Resiliency Hub that volunteers had set up as a command center was the calmest it had been in the past week. Music played, tinfoil crinkled as volunteers wrapped hot meals and people took turns answering phones almost constantly.
Volunteers and community leaders, including Nikki Richardson-Iwegbu, are staffing a Resiliency Hub in Kansas City, Kansas, where people needing assistance with food replacement, electrical repairs or medical help can call or visit. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
The group coordinated more than 250 volunteers, raised more than $22,500, and received more than 300 requests, which community members could fill out and submit to volunteers for help with food, debris and medical assistance. 
The Unified Government of Wyandotte County and the National Weather Service confirmed Wednesday that no one died or suffered major injuries as a result of the storm.
One day after the storm, the Unified Government of Wyandotte County released resources for community members needing assistance with damage, power outages, debris disposal, overnight shelter, food and medical issues.
Two days after the storm, Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly issued a state of disaster emergency proclamation, unlocking state resources to help local agencies. 
“We know the people of Wyandotte County are facing a long road to recovery after these devastating storms,” Kelly said. “Our priority is making sure residents have the support and resources they need to safely clean up, restore power, and begin rebuilding. The state of Kansas will continue working closely with local officials and emergency responders to help this community recover.”
Nearly one week after the storm, the Kansas National Guard began assisting with debris removal Wednesday in Wyandotte County, according to the Adjutant General’s Office, bringing three dump trucks, two front-end loaders, 15 chainsaws, and 43 Army and Air Guard personnel.
On Wednesday, Kansas Adjutant General Paul Schneider, the state’s senior military administrative officer, praised the community organizations’ efforts, saying they were doing an “outstanding job” of helping residents and small businesses. He said roughly 200 homes remained without power.
From left, Nikki Richardson-Iwegbu, Kansas City, Kansas Mayor Christal Watson, and Kansas Adjutant General Paul Schneider meet on Aug. 21, 2026, in to assess tornado-like storm damage northeast Kansas City, Kansas. (Photo by Matt Kleinmann)
He told a committee of state legislative leaders that debris removal will be “the long pole in the tent,” predicting it could take up to 60 days to fully clear the neighborhoods’ streets of tree logs and limbs, rubble from houses and buildings and other damage. 
“They have a long way to go,” he said.
Richardson-Iwegbu said volunteers were doing everything they could to shorten that timeline.
Since Saturday, teams have removed about 7,500 cubic yards of debris, Schneider said. 
Early indications point to the possibility of the storm’s damage exceeding the threshold for making federal disaster declaration requests, he said, which could permit assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
Schneider also requested $10 million in emergency disaster funding to address a “critical disaster fund resourcing shortfall,” which state officials approved unanimously.
Kansas currently has eight open state of disaster emergencies and 17 open major presidential disaster declarations. Roughly $5.6 million of the request will go toward reimbursing local jurisdictions and agencies that deployed under the state’s official policy group when responding to a disaster. Only about 50% of entities have submitted reimbursement packages, but the Kansas Department of Emergency Management already incurred the costs of reimbursement, making immediate funding critical, Schneider said. 
Initial assessments show that the storm in north Kansas City, Kansas, caused the second-most expensive amount of damage this year with nearly $1.5 million in reimbursement requests, according to records from the Kansas Adjutant General’s Office. The most expensive natural disaster damage this year came from wildland fires in May in western Kansas,
Schneider said the emergency management department never truly leaves the disaster response and recovery phase anymore.
“Over the last six to seven years, disaster response has become our operational norm,” Schneider said. 
The increasing frequency and intensity of natural disasters is one of the major reasons why Richardson-Iwegbu emphasized the importance of education and preparedness as the community moves forward from the storm.
The next steps are crucial, said Shelley Coulter, a volunteer at the Resiliency Hub and the executive director of neighborhood revitalization nonprofit Groundwork NRG.
She and Richardson-Iwegbu agree that equipping community members with the know-how and resources necessary to survive the next surprise storm will be the only way to sustain their community long-term. 
“How are we going to ensure environmental and human justice without education?” Coulter said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: The Battle of Lake Ontario: Trump opens a new front in the war on things with names
description: There are moments in American history when you can almost hear the machinery of government grinding toward a solution. This is not one of them. Michigan has plenty of problems that could use Washington’s attention. Families are getting mugged at the checkout counter by high prices. Michigan manufacturers are getting squeezed by another round of […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office on August 6, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)There are moments in American history when you can almost hear the machinery of government grinding toward a solution.
This is not one of them.
Michigan has plenty of problems that could use Washington’s attention. Families are getting mugged at the checkout counter by high prices. Michigan manufacturers are getting squeezed by another round of tariffs on Canadian goods. Communities are still living with the poisoned legacy of the Flint Water Crisis, while PFAS contamination continues to threaten drinking water in communities across the state.
In other words, Michigan has actual water problems. Problems involving the water we drink. Not what we call a lake.
But with all of that demanding attention, Donald Trump has decided that his top priority should be renaming Lake Ontario as some sort of “gotcha” toward the Canadian government, which has the gall to stand up for its sovereignty. 
Trump has ordered federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” because apparently the best way to conduct trade negotiations with Canada is to pick an idiotic fight with a body of water. That’ll show ‘em. Nevermind that the province of Ontario is named after the lake and not the other way around. Clearly, facts mean little in all of this.
Regardless, we can all breathe easier knowing someone is tackling the important stuff. Forget lowering prices. Forget public health. Forget doing something, anything, to better the lives of our citizens. That would require actual work. Better to sign a meaningless piece of paper that most of the rest of the world will surely ignore.
New tariffs on Canada heighten Michigan Democrats’ affordability attacks on Trump, GOP

For Michigan, this would be funny if the consequences weren’t so damn serious. Because Canada isn’t some faraway country that Michiganders encounter only on a map.
Canada is right there.
Detroit looks across the river at Windsor. Michigan and Ontario are connected by roads, bridges, tunnels, pipelines, power grids, supply chains and decades of economic cooperation.
Michigan businesses depend on Canadian trade. Michigan workers depend on Canadian-connected industries. And millions of Michiganders live in a state whose economy and identity are inseparable from the Great Lakes.
So when Washington picks an economic fight with Canada, Michigan doesn’t get to sit this one out.
Instead, we get the bill.
The Trump administration’s latest tariffs on Canadian goods threaten to raise costs for consumers and squeeze businesses on both sides of the border. Michigan Democrats are already hammering Republicans over affordability, and it’s not difficult to understand why. 
When you slap a massive tax on goods coming from one of your largest trading partners, somebody eventually pays.
Spoiler alert: It’s you.
It’s the family buying groceries. The worker putting gas in the car. The manufacturer paying more for inputs. The small business trying to survive another round of economic whiplash.
But don’t worry.
The lake has been renamed.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And now comes the most embarrassing part: watching Republican politicians scramble to decide whether they should cheer this nonsense or simply pretend it never happened.
Some dutifully applaud, eager to demonstrate their loyalty to Trump no matter how ridiculous the spectacle. Others will attempt the political equivalent of the Homer Simpson meme — slowly backing into the bushes and hoping nobody notices them disappearing. And who can blame them? When the president picks a fight with a lake, the safest political position is to say nothing. But cravenness in service of party loyalty is the exact opposite of what we need from our leaders.
What’s worse, and frankly unforgivable, is that Michigan is uniquely exposed to the consequences of a thoughtless trade war .
This state has spent generations building an economy around cross-border commerce. We don’t just trade with Canada — we build things together. 
Parts cross the border. Energy crosses the border. Workers cross the border. Products cross the border. Families cross the border.
Before 9/11, teens occasionally crossed the border because Canada has a lower drinking age.
At least, that’s what I’ve heard. Strictly journalism here.
Anyway, the point is that the relationship is so deeply woven into Michigan life that the international border can sometimes feel less like a wall and more like a seam. Trump keeps trying to turn that seam into a battlefield.
And then, apparently, he looks at the Great Lakes and thinks: You know what this needs? Branding.
A trade war isn’t a television show. Tariffs aren’t applause lines. They are taxes that work their way through supply chains until they eventually land in someone’s budget.
So while Trump is busy declaring that a lake needs a more patriotic name, Michigan businesses are left wondering what the next tariff will cost them.
And consumers are wondering why everything costs so damn much. And public-health officials are still dealing with measles.
And Americans are still watching a war that shows no obvious interest in ending.
But hey — Lake America.
There is something almost poetic about it. A president confronted with enormous, complicated problems has chosen the one solution that requires absolutely no competence whatsoever.
If the name fits…

Crime scene tape surrounds an entry to the Barus & Holley engineering building at Brown University on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Providence’s response to the December 2025 mass shooting at Brown University was “highly effective” and “decisive,” according to an independent review commissioned by Mayor Brett Smiley earlier this year. 
But the 76-page report published Friday by the Washington, D.C.-based Police Executive Research Forum (PERF) also identified gaps in communication and coordination among local, university, state and federal law enforcement agencies that city officials should address before another large-scale emergency.
“While these issues did not undermine the response, personnel often had to rely on experience, relationships, and real-time adaptation to work through these gaps,” the report states. “Providence is well positioned not only to build on its performance in this incident but to serve as a model for other jurisdictions seeking to strengthen their preparedness for complex, high-consequence events.”
Smiley on Feb. 19 commissioned Police Executive Research Forum to conduct the assessment at a cost of $95,000, saying at the time that it would help identify “what worked well and where we must improve in training, tools, tactics and technology” after the Dec. 13 shooting killed two students and wounded nine others during an economics final review in Brown’s Barus & Holley building.
“It’s really important that the community not just hear from us, but hear from a national expert of where we did well and where we can do better,” Smiley reiterated in an interview ahead of the report’s release.
The authors of third party consultants’ report’s authors interviewed Providence police personnel, reviewed investigative materials related to the incident, and analyzed publicly available documents. 
Brown University is conducting its own after-action review and campus safety and security assessment with the global consulting firm Teneo. 
“Our semester begins shortly, and we are finalizing release plans and timing now,” Brian Clark, a spokesperson for the Ivy League university, said in an email.
The U.S. Department of Education launched a probe into university security measures in late December. A department spokesperson declined to comment on the status of its “ongoing” investigation.
What city got right
The report found the city’s response times “met or exceeded” national benchmarks established for active-shooter incidents. 
Providence police arrived on scene less than three minutes after dispatch at 4:07 p.m. and “did not hesitate to enter the Barus & Holley building despite not knowing whether the shooter was still inside.” Officers evacuated all nonfatally injured victims by 4:23 p.m.
Active-shooter benchmarks generally call for all victims to be transported within 30 minutes, according to the report. 
“Those first minutes were about one thing: saving lives,” Police Chief Col. Oscar Perez said in a statement. “Their response was swift, courageous and focused on protecting life and securing the scene in the midst of an extraordinarily dangerous situation.”
The report recommended the city maintain its Flock automated license-plate reader (LPR) camera system, even as concerns over privacy and misuse have flared up throughout the state. Smiley said he supports the suggestion, calling it a valuable tool integral to the investigation.
“But it’s a tool that needs to be used appropriately, and data sharing needs to be strictly enforced and regularly audited,” he said.
Investigators used the Flock cameras to narrow the search for the suspected shooter’s vehicle after receiving multiple tips, most notably a Dec. 15 post on Reddit directing police to look for a “grey Nissan with Florida plates, possibly a rental.”
“LPR data proved indispensable, reducing an investigative universe of thousands of potential vehicles to just two in a matter of minutes,” the report states.
Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, a Portuguese national who briefly attended Brown in 2000, walked away from the crime scene, launching a five-day manhunt that involved local, state and federal law enforcement. Neves Valente, who also shot and killed a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor two days after the Brown shooting, was found dead in a storage locker in Salem, New Hampshire on Dec. 18. 
The review also praised city officials for how they handled media inquiries, particularly after police detained a person of interest on Dec. 14, a man who was released later that same day. Perez was described as “circumspect” for sharing only verified facts and declining to label the individual as a suspect. Smiley, who oversaw each of the city’s press conferences, was seen as “measured and highly effective” with his public communication. 
A Providence police cruiser is seen parked on Brook Street about a block north of the Barus & Holley building on Sunday, Dec. 14, 2025, the day after a gunman killed two students and injured nine others at Brown University. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
What went wrong
The report identified the lack of integration between Brown’s surveillance system and the city’s. 
Investigators initially struggled to determine what campus cameras and other video resources were available. Which is why the Police Executive Research Forum recommends the university add its camera network into the city’s Real Time Crime Center, where detectives can access live feeds from hundreds of cameras to gather “actionable” information to rapidly respond to incidents.
Smiley said conversations with the university remain ongoing for camera connections.
Broader public communication drew criticism at the time. Some neighborhood residents lamented the lack of emergency 311 notifications during and after the shooting.
Smiley initially rebuffed criticisms, saying the city’s alert system worked as intended for everyone who signed up. The mayor now acknowledges that “some neighbors felt like they were inadequately notified” and that the city has since worked to improve communication in the event of another emergency.
He said Providence has since revamped its CodeRED notification system to push emergency messages to residents without an audible alarm. The report notes that at the time of the shooting, the system was inoperable, which led to some partner agencies not receiving timely awareness of key developments during the early phases of the response.
One example came inside the Barus & Holley building as Providence police and campus officers entered the building from different locations without initially knowing the other agency was inside. Their communications were integrated only after they physically encountered one another, a situation the report noted “carried inherent risk.”
“Obviously, that didn’t happen, and everything worked out in terms of their safety and their willingness to respond quickly,” Smiley said. “But that’s an area that we went to address and fix very quickly.”
Smiley said direct contact between Brown and local police leaders increased after former Providence Police Chief Hugh T. Clements Jr. assumed daily oversight of campus policing in late December.
